Smile(' as Mks. Cole enteeed., - • • 'F. "Oh, I'm so glad you've come back," she said. \ "That—that—madman has returned. I have not seen him, though already he has asked to see me, says he has something of importance to impart to me. I absolutely won't see hfin alone. And I've written to Jack." 1 Mrs. Cole sat down.
"To say what ? " she

asked. "To say he must come 'lime. I'm very sorry, but I'm not going to be worried out of my life, and I don't believe Jack has ever done anything discreditable. Any way, I shall ask him." "Ask your brother?" "Yes." Mrs. Cole laughed. "My dear child," she .said, "do you suppose any man or woman in the world would acknowledge they had done any- thing discreditable ? Not they! But don't worry. The game of life is very much like a game of cards; the last trump, however small, takes the , trick. Leave Vernon Salisbury to me. I hold the last trump card. He has never really come into your life, but he shall certainly go-out of it!" "What do you mean?" " Ah! that I can't tell you. We all have our , secrets. I must 'keep mine. Keep clear of a ttte-h-tete conversation with Vernon Salisbury until I have interviewed him. After that, I ; think, you will find "—she laughed quite merrily— "that he did not know what he was talking about when he said he loved you; had any desire to marry you; meant to frighten Mr. John into compelling you to be his wife." "You mean-- ?" Olive paused, looked puzzled. "I mean by eleven o'clock to-night, if I am ' not very much mistaken, I shall be affianced to Vernon Salisbury. For reasons into which it is not necessary to enter we shall go abroad. you'll laugh at me, I daresay, think I'm a foolish woman. I can't help it. I'm very much in love with him, and a woman is a fool if she ; does not marry the man with whom she is in love, if shd can. It doesn't always spell lifelong: happiness, I know, but it does spell moments of perfect bliss, and that's more than most of us I get out of life." Olive rose, went to Mrs. Cole, and kissed her. "You've taken a load off my mind," she said. "I ; have sent a message to Mr. Salisbury that I cannot ! see him. You really think you can manage him ? " Once more Mrs. Cole laughed. "My dear • child, I don't think," she answered, "I am sure— quite sure. Don't. worry, leave everything to me. You and I have always been good friends. I'm going to be a little more now. I'm going to be your good angel, and I hope my own." Quite unconscious of all Mrs. Cole knew or thought she knew, Vernon Salisbury mapped out his own plans. John Brandon had refused absolutely to influence his sister in the convict's favour, but that individual, nothing daunted, meant to play his own cards. Women, he told himself, were more timid, mere easily influenced than men. He would only have to threaten her brother with the gallows, to bring Olive, metaphorically speaking, to her knees at once. And that was what- he would do. His position with'her, too, Would be far stronger than it was with her brother, because she knew nothing of his past; had not the slightest idea he was the convict—the man for whom everyone almost was scouring the ,country. So far as she knew he was an old friend of-John's, home from Australia. "Women," he said to himself, "are proverbially timid for others, though brave enough so far as they themselves are concerned. I shall give no details, of course, no dates. I shall just mention the fact, which is a fact and the absolute truth, that her brother has committed' murder—that, unless she consents to become my wife, I shall give him up to justice, and she will drop into my arms like a ripe peach." He was so sure of his ground that he was not even vexed when, in answer to his message, a maidservant told him Miss Brandon was engaged, and could not see him. He rather gloated over the girl's disinclination to cone to him; in some natures is planted a, big seed of cruelty. it seemed to him it was almost as pleasant that she should think of him with fear and trembling as with love. "And she'll fear and tremble more when I tell her all I have to tell," he thought, "when I force her against her will to be mine—my wife— mine utterly. And slowly the fear and trembling will leave het; gradually she will become glad that she is mine, and I am hers. I shall drink the cup of life's emotion to its very dregs, and the lost di aught will be the sweetest." • Olive Brandon had said he was mad. Perhaps fcr the time-being Ire-IVas alittle off Ins -neaa with emotional imaginings. He had forgotten altogether his own danger, that he might be re-taken at ally .inoment, condemned once more to the death in life of a convict prison. 1-Jo walked in the garden, but he saw no one. He did not care for her in the least, but he would have been glad even of the company of, Mrs. Cole. At six o'clock he once more sought his room to dress for dinner.. John Brandon's ' tailor had fitted him with clothes, in -which knew he looked remarkably well. With as much vanity as a young girl he looked ! at himself in the glass, and smiled as he told him- self—which was perfectly true—that he was quite as good-looking as Paul Clifford. .He forgot, however, that women do not always love with their eyes. Sometimes it is with their eyes—sometimes it is with their hearts. Five minutes before the hour for dinner he went downstairs, to find Mrs. Cole alone in the drawing-room. He noticed she was looking hand- somer than ever. It seemed to him, also, that she looked at him strangely. He wondered why. "So you have come back," Mrs. Cole said. "We have been wondering very much, Miss Brandon and I, for what reason you. could have wished to see Mr. Brandon. I should think she smiled archly—"he was not overjoyed to pee you, was lie? I, as you of course know, have experienced one honeymoon. I think my late husband would almost have killed anyone who had intruded upon us." "So jealous ?" he asked, carelessly. He was not in the least interested in her or her late husband. "So human, she corrected. "Put yourself in Mr. Brandon's place. Would you care to have a man friend rushing upon you, breaking into your paradise, your Garden of Eden?" He looked at her with a little interest, and laughed. "In Jack's place, I should not have mincfed in the least," Ile answered, "because in Jack's place I should not crave for a solitude a deux. I don't much admire his bride." "But with the bride 30bu did admire—love ? • "Ah! that would be a different pair of shoes, -would it not? Well, to tell you the truth, Jack was not at all pleased to see me, and did not in the least disguise his feelings. I wonder "—he looked round—" when Miss Brandon is coming? I have not seen her since I came back." Mrs. Cole took up a book, turned over its pages slowly, though she did not see a word or a picture. . "She will come down when the dinner gong sounds," she said. "Miss Brandon, as you no doubt know, is in that delightful condition of selfish enjoyment, that when she is not with one particular individual, she prefers to be alone. Love's young dream is sweetest, no doubt, dreanat in one society or the one beloved, but Moo absolutely precious dreamt in solitude." "You mean "—he drew hi's breath rather hard —"that Miss Brandon is in love ? " She lifted her eyebrows in feigned suprise. "Why, of course," she answered. "Do you mean you have lived in the same house with her and not discovered that? Wen, for unnatural blind- ness, commend me to a man! In love !—she is fathoms deep in love—and, of course, she and Mr. Clifford are engaged—are only waiting until Mr. Brandon returns to announce their engage- ment." A smile curved his handsome lips. "I don't think that engagement will be announced," he said. "I think you will find John Brancicn has other views for her future." The door opened and Olive Brandon entered the room. As she did so Vernon Salisbury went quickly to meet her. clasped her hand closely

div.head: WRITTEN IN SCARLET.
div.p: WRITTEN IN SCARLET.
BY ALICE MAUD MEADOWS, Author of "One Life Between," "A Million cf Money," "The Extreme. Penalty," "For Love fof a Lady," "I Charge You Both," Su),
CHAPTER XX.VIII. MRS. COLE MAKES UP HER MIND.

As soon as Olive returned to her lover Mrs. Cole put on a shady hat, and strolled in an aimless way down to the vill§ge. When she came to the police,station she dait her eyes along the bills and notices. She saw at-once that at the far end of the hoarding one bill bore a like- ness—the likeness, no doubt, of the escaped. convict. For all that she did not hurry towards it, but took things in a leisurely manner, reading each notice. An inspector came out from the station as she reached the big bill, touched his hat, and joined her. _
"Having a look at our picture gallery ? " he said, smilingly. "I wish we could take that last bill down.'

He pointed to one which was headed "Escaped from Dartmoor Prison," and went on to give not only a description but a portrait of No. 27. Mrs. Cole looked at it a trifle shyly. It seemed to her it bore a strong likeness to Vernon Salisbury, though she would, perhaps, not have noticed it had not suspicion already been in her mind.

"You wish you could take it down?" she repeated. "Yes," he answered. "He'd be caught then. We can't take it down till he's caught. It's most extraordinary where the man is hiding. It's morally certain he has not left this place; every station, and road, and port in England has been 'watched. I hardly think he can have got rid of his convict's dress even. There was a rumour the other night that old Dignal was hiding him. He had a sick man there, it seems, who has gpne off his head, and who, overhearing a con- versation relating to taking an escaped convict, imagined he was the man, and made off. He, also has not been found again. Old Dignal is in a fine state about him, but it seems pretty certain he's not our man. I wish he had been; though in a way I should have been sorry, because that fool of a Warder Clark would have had all the honour and glory of catching him." • Mrs. Cole looked at the portrait of the convict. wonder if that is like the man ? " she said.

The inspector's glance followed hers. "I don't know. I suppose it is in a way," he said, "though, naturally, these likenesses are not very good. The description would probably help one more in laying one's hands on him. That seems to me to be very distinctive. If I could clap eyes on the man I should know him fast enough." _ _ _

He read the description half-aloud as be spoke. Feature for feature, once more, it seemed to Mrs. Cole it was like Vernon Salisbury, all excepting the hair; and if Paul Clifford was right Vernon Salisbury wore a wig. She looked at the inspector and smiled. "I'm • afraid," she said, ai feel a certain amount of sympathy with this man." He nodded affably. "That goes without saying," he answered. "I don't know why it is —it's for their protection such men are shut up— but the general public always is sympathetic towards an escaped convict. It's the sporting instinct, I suppose, and I don't know that it's a bad trait in the national character. In my official capacity, of course, I -wish such folk re-taken. In private life, I suppose, I sympathise with a man who has made such a plucky dash for liberty. We are most of us complex, two- Sided, if not more, in our character." Mrs. Cole turned'away fi-orl,the notinpg. - -"I wonder,wilat, the man has done?- " she said. "Not murder, I hope ? " _ _

The inspector shook his head. "No. not murder," he returned. "He'd have been h •_;.A or put in Broadmoor if he'd committed murder, though, in a way, he perhaps did worse. He swindled hundreds of folks with a bogus friendly society, or something of that sort. Of course, he pleaded that he was unfortunate not criminal —you must remember the Rosco-INfordaunt Case —however, the judge and jury thought other- wise."
Mentally Mrs. Cole looked at Vernon Salisbury's handsome face, heard his charming voice.

"They may have been mistaken," she said. "Justice has miscarried before now. Well, Inspector, T. suppose I must not keep you any Longer. Good-day to you." "Good-day to you, ma'am," the inspector answered, and touched his hat as he moved off. Just as the sun's rays in August are a very different thing from the sun's rays in May or June, so the love of a middle-aged woman is very different from that of a young girl. Mrs. Cole had wished to marry John Brandcn, but she had fallen violently in love with Vernon Salisbury. That he did not love her, that he was, without doubt, an escaped convict, a man with a price upon his head, a criminal, mattered to her very little, if at all. Just as a man will often crave passionately for a woman whom he knows to be unworthy of love so she wanted iis man utterly in her life. And now, though The knew he did not love her, it seemed to her if she chose she could have him. "And I do choose," she said to herself. "After all, what is a fraud? It may be a mere misfor- tune; some wild-cat schemes go right for years, some go wrong at once. The lucky, man pulls it off, the unlucky man gets sent to prison. I daresay he's no more guilty of swindling the public than plenty of folk who sit in high pl RCM " She made her way home feeling pretty well satisfied. She had a small income of her own left her by her late husband; she had saved since she had been one of the household of John Brandon, saved a good deal. She had been given almost carte blanche in the matter of spending for household purposes, and had not forgotten to feather her own nest. Her salary, too, had been liberal, and it had never been necessary to touch that. For this reason, perhaps, though she would ,ertainly not have confessed as much to herself, fraud did not seem to her a very terrible thing. More or less, she told herself, everyone was a fraud. She wondered what possible hold this man could have on John Brandon. Any way, whatever it was, it could, perhaps, be turned to account. If she took the convict out of her employer's way, surely he would be grateful. "A girl would be afraid to marry him." she said to herself. "It is very little of which Jam afraid. We will leave England together, and until he loves me, which will be in tiire, 1 shall be quite happy in loving him. After all, it is greater joy, just as it is more blessed, to give than to receive." , She was not, perhaps, of a very refined nature. It did not seem to her an Immodest and monstrous thing that through, fear she should force herself on a man. She l'l long wished for another husband. The life sfie had been living now for a good many years was distasteful to her. She wanted a home of her own. She had done her best to marry John --Brandon, and had failed. Here, willy-nilly, was a companion for life. She did not surely flatter herself unduly when she told herself a man would certainly prefer life as .her mate to a convict prison. "And it shall he one or the other, she said to herself, smiling grimly. "Ho deserves to be punished—if punishment it will be—for flirting with me, making a cat's-paw of me, when all the time he meant to force -Olive to be his wife. Well, well, it is a case of the biter bit indeed, or will be." She reached home, to find that Vernon Salisbury had returned and had gone to his room. She did not want to speak to him yet, she would wait eintil after cliuney. .She rooked her 1,‘,.t gasflgnt in a grana "GOMM he hact sufficient womanliness left to wish him to admire her, even if she did want to force his inclinations. • She made her way to Olive's room. The girl was sittino there alone. gala leelce.3 lin 2111
itna tnen canner was anuouncea.

Paul Clifford was not present, but, aa usual, he was coming in after dinner. Vernon Salisbury was not aware of the fact, but there was very little chance of his getting any private conversa- tion with Olive that night. Dinner, thanks to Mrs. Cole, passed off pleasantly., She was, and not unnaturally, excited; this made her looks, as well as her conversation, more than usually brilliant. iv As the ladies rose at length from the table, Paul Clifford knocked at the door, and an expres- sion of relief crossed Olive's face. She hurried away, met him in the hall, slipped her hand thyouch.liis arm. and smileil un into his faro —tome mtc tnb gtia. men, sue saw, "the night is too beautiful to be indoors. You don't want coffee very badly, do you ? " . .

"I don't wad it at -all," he answered. "I ask nothing better than to go out into the moonlight, into the gentle solitude of the night with you." Mrs. Cole smiled to herself, and made her way into the drawing-room. It would not be long, she knew, before Vernon Salisbury followed them—as he thought. And then she would have her say. She would put things „plainly before him. She was certain, quite certain of her around; she also,knew what she wanted—which is more than half the folk in the world do, or more would get it.
She had iiot long to wait. She heard him coming with a quick, jaunty step, as she sipped her coffee. He looked disappointed when he saw she was alone.

"Miss Brandon is in the garden," she said. "Ah ! "—as he moved towards the window—"l do not think she wants you, Mr. Salisbury—Mr. Clifford is with her. Have you had COffee ? " "Thank you, yes," he answered. ' "I —I think I will join them; as a matter of fact, I have some- thing very particular to say to Miss Brandon— something private." Mrs. Cole leant comfortably back 'among the cushions. She looked at him through half-closed lids, noting his absolutely manly beauty,rejoicing in it A little smile played round her lips. "And I also have something private to say to you," she said. "That surprises you, doesn't it? I don't think it should, because during these weeks you have spent in this house I have had every right to believe you had something private to. say to me." He coloured hotly; he looked more than uncom- fortable. "I—don't understand," he answered. "But I think you should," she said, with perfect good temper. "I have concluded, of course, _that you knew—it is patent to everyone— that Miss Brandon and Mr. Clifford were engaged. You have paid me very great attention; you have been lavish with your compliments; you have, inadvertently perhaps, led me to suppose that you cared for me, and in return I have grown to care for you. Even now. "—she opened her eyes very wide, looked at him with a very direct glance— 'that 1. know your secret— who you are—whence you came—l still care for you—No. .27 ! " He sprang to his feet, • for a moment he utterly lost his nerve; then with a superhuman effort he 'regained it. "I —I (16 not understand," he said. "No. 27! he laughed nervously. "What do You mean ? " She leant towards him; she cared for him— was sorry for his fear. "You clO know what I mean," she answered. "You know perfectly well if I rang that bell and told, not my Suspicions, but my certainty, you would be back in Dartmoor Prison to-night. Oh! don't be frightened, I'm not going to ring the bell. It was not until-I heard you had been trying to frighten Olive into a marriage With you, that I had any suspicion—that I began to put two and two together—l knew "—she did not absolutely speak the truth—"that you wore a wig. I remembered my remarks When I read the description of the escaped convict that feature by feature it resembled you. I remembered also that you avoided seeing the prison warder. Little things came back to me—your arrival at the house unexpectedly on the night the prisoner escaped, no one but Mr. Brandon saw you come; you wore—oh," I noticed that—a suit of his clothes at the wedding ; you have since patronised his tailor. These are all little things, but they tell up. What the hold you have over him is I do not know; but of this I am determined 4 if you attempt to use it, you go back to prison. I don't wish you to, because—l am a fool, of course, but—l care for you. lam willing to marry you I am willing to leave England with you. You must not stop herei of course; I am not willing you should make the life of John Brandon or his sister unhappy. I've no doubt—not the.._slightest—hut that you ,do x-now siiingthing. against Mr. Brandon; did you not, he would never have harboured you. You shall make no use of that knowledge—at least, you will not if you are wise. I should fancy working in the quarries, in clothes liberally sprinkled with the broad arrow, can scarcely be pleasant to you!" He smiled almost offensively. "lam, of course, flattered by your proposal," he said, and for the first time the man betrayed the fact that he was really not a gentleman. "I am not going to deny the truth of what you say; but whether I fall in with your romantic plans or not, I do not think you will dare to betray inc. You have admitted a soft corner in your heart—or what you call your heart, which is probably your acute emotional capacity. Well "—he spoke very quietly—"l could hang John Brandon!" She turned 'suddenly very pale. It was curious, though John's life contradicted anything of the sort, that she believed him.

"What nonsense ! " she said, and her lips trembled. "But it is not nonsense!" he answered. "In the past—whether in the far-away or immediate past—John Brandon committed murder! I saw him do it. Give me up to prison, and I betray him. Why "—he lied for all he was worth—"do you suppose I could have bullied him into the promise that his sister should be my wife, if that were not true ? "
Ho had played too strong a card, he had over- reached himself—the woman's jealousy blazed up.,_

"What is John Brandon to m- e ! " sfie said. "If he has committed a crime, .what do I care if he suffers for it-? A life for a life is justice—all that has nothing to do with me; as for the rest —you can take my terms or leave them. You'll be a fool if you do not clutch at them. I've taken a fancy to you; convict though you are, I am willing to marry you. Think the thing out. You have pretended to love me, in the pretence there may have been some grain of truth. Let me know your decision to-morrow, and don't try to get away. I shall not betray you, but any secret attempt I shall circumvent. You may be too clever for the rest of the world, but you're not 'cute enough to out-manceuvre the woman who has the whip-hand of you." Vernon Salisbury shrugged his shoulders. "You talk of the whip-hand," he said, "and in the same breath you say you love me." t "And I do," she answered. "There is more than one kind of love—there is the love of the tiger as well as the love of the dove. I ought to despise you; my duty is to give you up to justice, but I can't do it—and I won't, unless you try to interfere with the lives of those here, who have been good friends to me for many years. I've heard all about your crime, and—you'll think that strange, perhaps—l don't think it so very terrible. You must make up your mind now as to what course I am to pursue—whether I am to be your friend or your foe; and mind "—her face softened—"l don't want to be your foe." .•, _ _

He hesitated more than a -minute. He had fallen in love, it was true, but not with Mrs. Cole; he wanted a woman in his life, but not this woman. Stilli there was no doubt whatever with regard to that—she had the whip hand. "Be my friend," he said, softly, "my best and nearest friend; since you care for me it will not be a very hard task for me to care for you. We will leave England together; no one will suspect your husband of being No. 27—oh! I admit I am he—and in the future I'll do my best to run straight, if only because I've found out the truth of the old adage—' Honesty is the best policy.'"
(To be concluded.)

LADIES TOO SUCCESSFUL.

The Salters' Company have decided that in future their annual travelling scholarship of £25 for proficiency in modern languages shall be limited to male students. The scholarship is in the hands of the Education Committee of the London Chamber of Commerce, and last year it was awarded to a lady student of Pitman's School, Southampton-row. The scholarship was established to encourage the British clerk in his competition with the numerous foreigners who are, willing to work for much smaller salaries. Up to the present about equal numbers of male and female students have competed on the same footing, but during the last eight years the scholarship has only once been won by a male student. The original object of the scholarship is in this way defeated, and so the City company has decided that its annual gift shall for the future be confined to male students, who are the persons really affected by the keen foreign com- petition. PRETTY PINAFORE.

Pictured in our illustration is the daintiest of little pinafores, suitable for smartening up a dark or plain nursery frock, or for wear as a pro- tection over a pretty " best " dress. This, chariping little pinafore is made of -nothing more costly than clear white muslin patterned with a tiny embroidered spot. Over the shoulders comes a smart little square yoke, made of alter-

nate bands of Valenciennes insertion and wee tucks. This yoke is bordered all round with a band of the Valenciennes insertion, and is finished at the top with a small frill of the same lace. The pinafore is gathered on to the yoke, and is allowed to ,hang quite loose, the hem be- ing adorned by a band of insertion. Over the Lops of the sleeves come frilled epaulettes of the muslin edged with the Valenciennes lace.

div.head: FANCIES OF FASHION,
div.p: FANCIES OF FASHION,

As alternative to the knitted silk motor scarf Dn one hand and a fur wrap on the other, cravat ties of chiffon velvet or chenille are pretty, par- ticularly in prune or old-rose. The smartest, says " Celia " in the Lady, have a narrow bor- lering of oxidised tinsel and a shaped frill of blond lace, and the muff corresponds. Steel bead trimming in strips is still adopted with zest, more especially as cuffs and narrow stole pieces for evening wraps of rich dark vel- vet. It accords well with a collar of chinchilla r ermine. Bands of thick " wool-work " em- broidery look well upon simple theatre coats of pastel faced cloth.

r Wine-red, olive-green, and brown - are the best-worn colours, the present moment being iistinctly dedicated to dark and neutral tones. Also there-- is a warm colour that has been .7leverly -described as "copper lustre." Embroidery will never suenopd in ousting lace from our affection for lingerie, yet so popular is broderie Anglaise that even corsets of fine batiste are decorated in pierced fashion. _

The necessary "swing at the hem of walk- ing skirts is imparted by means of an inverted box-pleat down the middle of both front and back, each stitched as far as the knees. Current millinery still demands the addition of curls set at various angles, the bunches which are mounted upon dainty combs proving com- fortable and secure.

div.head: SPRING COSTUME.
div.p: SPRING COSTUME.

The subject of our sketch is a neat and smart little costume suitable for wear throughout the coming spring. The material used for its achievement is a very pretty green-and-grey mixture tweed of light weight and rather loose weave. Over the shoulders of the coat, which, by the way, is rather suggestive of the " Nor- folk " in style, come stitched straps of the mate- rial, piped with green cloth, which are carried

right down to the bottom of the coat. From the neck turns back a smart little collar of green cloth edged with a strapping of the tweed. The coat fastens in double-breasted fashion, and is held in to the figure by a stitched band of the material, which passes under the stitched straps and fastens beneath the coat in front. The skirt is perfectly plain save for a shaped band of the material round the bottom, which comes up the front of the skirt and forms a panel. This shaped band is piped with the green cloth and machined at the edges.

Frank R. Ellis, of the American Book Com- pany, lived in Mount Auburn for a number of years, but last spring moved to another part of the city. The day appointed for the removal was a beautiful, sunny one, and Mr. Ellis was personally supervising the transfer of his house- hold possessions. Before his house stood three big moving-vans, and the lawn was almost' covered with furniture of various sorts, pic- tures, chinaware in crates, and other things. As Mr. Ellis stood directing the movers, a lady With whom he was acquainted passed, and smilingly asked: " Oh, Mr. Ellis, are you moving?" " Not at all, madam," he answered. " I am only taking my furniture out for a ride."

The plight of the Prince of 'Wales, in failing ,D get his special train to Madrid, and having a go on by "ordinary," is by no means the first ocasiou when the British Royal family have .aen in a similar predicament. The Duke of Oonnaught can remember the day when he and ho Duchess, with their children, arrived at lournemouth on a visit to a local granaee. Thy Irccitement of the event somewhat paralysed the oat's organising powers, and the carriages for he Royal guests not only were sent to the wrong station, but were despatched at the wrong .our. The Duke and Duchess grasped the situa- tion in a moment, and quietly took their seats ka a penny 'bus going an thr;direction of tbeit kost's residence. No one suspected their iden, lity.

A prison visitor recently asked one of the prisoners how he came to be there. "Want," was the answer. "How was that, pray?" "Well, I wanted another man's watch. He wasn't will- ing I should have it, and the judge wants me to stay here five years."

"So you can't help stealing?" asked the magis- trate kindly. "No, your worship; an impulse comes over Me that I can't resist." "Too bad, too bad! An impulse to send you to prison for six months is getting hold of me. There! It's got hold. Six months ; I can't resist. Impulse is a wonderful thing."

"I am afraid, madam,'7 said a gentleman who was looking for country lodgings, "that the house is too near the station to be pleasant." "It, is a. little assented the landlady, "but from the front verandah one has such a fine view of people who miss the trains."

and Mr. Triggs and party would -have stared had they beheld the charming smile by which the words were accompanied. Their recipient did not stare, he only blushed very shyly and deeply, as lads of seventeen, Sensi- tive to kindness, more particularly feminine kind- ness, do blush at times. Then he tried to speak, finding it equally hard to find something to say, and when found, to say it. "But I couldn't, that is to say, I can't. I mean I couldn't, you know." "Oh, yes, I think you can," said the lady, "A-course you can," nodded Dorothy, frowning. She had hold of his hand and was not going to let it g 9. The last four hours had been to her a species of Elysium. Ashamed and disgraced she had fled from the presence of her tormentors, for, child as she was, she had perceived in -what light they regarded her sufferings, and resented the grudging reluctance,alwost worse than a refusal, accorded to her mother's appeal. Her heart swelling with mortification and amazement, and her eyes blinded by a burst of tears, she had heard the cruel laugh which mocked her retreating steps, and, strange to say, it had acted like a tonic. What with indigna- tion, tears, and the blast of fresh air in the passage, giddiness and nausea, where were they? Gone. But where was Dorothy? Literally sobbing her heart out in the arms of a lanky lad, an utter stranger, who had been looking out of the passage window, and against whom she had stumbled in her headlong flight. She would have fallen but that he caught her. "What's the matter ? " said he. "Don't cry, little girl. Poor little girl, don't cry." -Then he , stroked her hair, and patted her shoulder, and saw , nothing of another figure in the passage, who checked her impulse to interfere, and held back watching. "Agustin' people," sobbed Dorothy. "Poor little girl," said the lad again. He had the gentlest voice imaginable, and he took out his own pOcket-handkerchief and tenderly wiped away the fast raining tears as they fell. "Em laughed at me," whispered the offended little one, catching her breath between each word. "Em did—oh, oh, oh ! " "Did they? Well, never mind. See bow nice it is out here," and, with instinctive tact, he created diversion for her thoughts. "It is quite cool here, and you are so hot," holding-a small swollen hand into the current of air. "Isn't .that nice ? " "Ess, you're kind, aren't you ? " smiles breaking out again. "Where's my muvver ? " said Dorothy, suddenly looking round. She was apparently gazing from a window a few feet off. "That's her," said Dorothy, contentedly. All was right, now, she thought. "Shall I take you to her ? " suggested her new friend. Dorothy, looked at him; her cheeks were still glazed with tears but the blue eyes shone, and all the friendliness of a sociable little soul was at work. "Rather stay with you," said she; and then, glancing suggestively towards some portmanteaux piled in the passage: "Won't you take me on your knee ? "

And fast asleep upon his knee, with her fair skirls streaming over his shoulder and his long arms firmly clasped round her, Dorothy's mother presently found her. She was not a very quick- witted woman, but maternal instinct had guided her under the present circumstances. So she merely' smiled and nodded at the schoolboy, and he understood that he might obey his little mistress's behest. At the end of half-an-hour, however, being really unable any longer to stand, and yet dreading beyond everything to go back to her seat, the young lady—for she was still a young lady, whatever George Triggs might have thought—stole along the passsage. Oh, dear, what was this? An empty compartment, right opposite to where the piled portmanteaux made a seat for Dorothy and her friend. "Is this where you are sitting ? " .whispered the lady, softly. He motioned assent. "And no one else?" "They got out at Carlisle." "And may—oh, may we come in ?." It was the gate of Paradise opening. "Only I don't like to disturb her," said the lad, looking down at his charge as he spoke. "She's sleeping so beautifully." Between them, however, they lifted the little slumberer on to the seat, and laid her down with her. I. ..a <4 soft "plaid. - There she slept on, and her two guardians talked and talked. Long before they had reached the point at which we took them up, when the train was approaching its destination for each alike, Dorothy's mother had learnt all about Dorothy's friend, and he had wondered at himself for being so ready to te,12.2... usually he was reserved with strangers. But there was no resisting the sweet face and winning manner. She learnt that he was alone in the world, and, albeit so *young, earning his own livelihood. He had got his holiday—a fortnight's holiday—and he thought he would like to come to Scotland—was fond of fishing; a friend had said there was fishing to be had at a certain place, and given the address; he fumbled in his pocket and brought it out. , "Really? That is where I am going too," said the lady, laughing outright. And then and there a thought arose, which presently was put into words. "You must, indeed; you must come home with us, with Dorothy and me," she said. "Home ? " The lonely boy's eyes emitted one eager flash; then he drew back timid and blushing, murmuring he knew not what. "We can give you better fishing than what you could get at the hotel," said the lady, gaily. "I wasn't thinking of going to the hotel. I thought perhaps I could get a room at a cottage somewhere," he replied. •Hotel bills were not for his modest purse. "So you can with us, with my husband and me. He will meet us at the station, and invite you. He always asks anyone I ask. Highland hospitality, you know." . • "You are—you are most awfully kind. But-- but I should take -up the room." In his mind's eye he saw a minute shooting-lodge, already brim- ing over; in hers—but no matter. She was more and more pleased with him every moment. He was so gentle, so truthful, so unassuming; and, absolutely ignorant as he was, he had rendered her such a service. She stuck to her point, and at length prevailed. • "We had got in with such very objectionable people," she had just began to confide, when suddenly the burly form of Mr. George Triggs • darkened the doorway. ("I'll look along and see where she has found a roost," he had told his com- panions, having lain low until now. "And I suppose I had, better take her bag to. her, eh?") Accordingly the bag was now tendered, with a "Hope the little gun's all right ? " in Mr. Triggs most supercilious and impressive drawl. . He was a little startled however by its reception. The lady who had just got as far as "objection- able people" turned in her seat, dropped her eye- lashes over her cheeks, and slowly raised her chin. , Her "Thank you" was haughtiness itself. I "Offended, by Jore ! " muttered he to himself; but he retreated-,somewhat . hastily, with a curious sense of discomfiture. He threw himself half out of the window, whistling; for the train was slowing to a standstill, and presently he called his women to look out. "I say—that's the Duke of Thingum- tight's—that big place up there. The guard says so, and that's one of his carriages waiting. There must be some of them in the train. Let's see them get out," and he turned the handle of the door, and was out on the platform in an instant, Mrs. and Miss Triggs following. ; ("Would you allow us to pass, please ? " A voice from behind. "Oh, certainly,". said George. ("She's getting out here, is she? And then he nearly had a fit upon the spot. He could never talk about it after- wards. And he never saw exactly what happened —but all in a moment there was a small hubbub on the spot. A powdered footman had seized his lady's bag— ow well George knew the brut I—. Vrpe,,t..*...4,1

was cnarieriiig aliu gesticulaturg, wildly apolOgetic end explanatory; Dorothy still firmly holding by her new friend's hand, was endeavouring to present him to a stalwart young Highlander in full costume —"A swell of swells," muttered the wretched Cockney, biting his lips, while this same great good-humoured fellow, laughing and kissing his wife (the widow!) demanded energetically, and without paying the slightest attention to anyone else, where in the name of wonder she had hidden herself? He had been up and down the platform and could find her nowhere.

"We had to get in where we could, Carlo; we were landed among such dreadful, dreadful people." (They heard her say it, distinctly heard her, though she, to do her justiee, knew not they were so pear. ) _

Was all a muddle," continued the speaker, eagerly. "Hortense got separated from Dorothy and me; and we, all by ourselves, were—oh, never mind. But—oh yes, of course "—her eye fell oil tho stranger lad: "Mr. James Stephens, Ctrlo. He is coming to stop with us. Your father will give him some fishing.' A whisper in his ear. The next minute Lord Charles was shaking the boy's hand heartily. "Where are your trays? Just point them out, will you? And he indicating the returning footman, "will send them up with ours. You come along with us," linking on to his arm. "My wife says you made friends on the way." And this too was plainly audible to the miserable Triggs trio. Oh; had they only "made friends on the way" also Nor did their punishment end here. A week later, all the world within hail was assembled to witness a Highland gathering on the outskirts of the town where the party had found quarters. They did all they could. They turned out in plaids and scarves, and white heather; strutted hither and thither wherever they could get, and looked longingly at the coaches and unapproachable grandees—but they felt themselves mean and small, and almost wished they had never come after one dreadful moment. It chanced that they passed the Duke's own special coach at the moment when a Lank, red-headed lad was pouring out a glass of champagne for a lady in black (but with a rosette of the clan tartan on her breast), and as they lingered, for even in torment they could not resist Lingering, they saw His Grace himself lean down and—" And give him a plate of pie," quoth George. Confound it!" and he pulled his deerstalker over his eyes to shut out the sight. "I never was played such a trick in my life," he muttered. But he did not see that it was he him- self who had played the trick. [THE END.

div.head: SCOTCH EXPRESS
div.p: THE SCOTCH EXPRESS
BY MRS. WALFORD,
Author of "Mr. Smith," "Dick Netherly," "Iva Kildare," "The Matchmaker," "A Bubble," "Ploughed," &c.

There were three of them, and they hq,d written beforehand to secure three corner seats in a third- class corridor compartment of the Scotchexpreas, which, luck befriending them, they had to them- selves•as far as Preston.

"Knew it was the tip to go by this line," quoth George, with a knowing chuckle, whereat his com- panions chuckled-back and thought what a fine follow they had got for a George and how splendid a thing it was to belong to him. At Preston they got out and lunched, and anyone who had the felicity of knowing Mr. George Triggs and his jolly little wife and jollier still little sister, may be sure they "did" themselves handsomely in this respect, and returned with satisfied, shining countenances to the compartment which by this time they had come to look upon as their own. They had indeed littered it freely, and the ladies had taken off their hats, while Mr. Triggs stretched his full length on the opposite -seat pre- paratory to a snooze, when "Confound it all !" mutters he, staring angrily round, for a porter, stupid ass! has opened the door and is looking interrogatively within. "This carriage is engaged," says Mr. Triggs, loftily. But the porter looks over his shoulder, and behind him stands the guard. "Tickets, please." They have only three tickets. "Can't engage a compartment for three tickets. Train's full," observed the guard, curtly. "Get in here, ma'am," aid, despite the reluctance with which the knickerbockered legs are withdrawn from their resting-place and the united scowls of the trio, two other passengers are almost flung in upon them, for the Scotch express has no time to waste and its guard no temper to lose in bandying words, during the early days of August.

A whistle and the train is off. The intruders have scarcely seated themselves, scanty space being accorded them to do so; and it is as well they have brought no paraphernalia, nothing beyond a small handbag which the lady places upon her knee, and doll which the child who nestles beside her hugs in her arms, for not an inch of room beyond what is absolutely required do they get. Mr. and Miss Triggs overhaul the new-corners disdainfully. A tiresome woman with a still more tiresome child. How odious, how disgusting Couldn't they have got in anywhere else? There must be compart- ments with other, children in them. Under pretence of altering the window blind Mrs. Trigga murmurs a suggestion to her husband : "Why shouldn't he go along the 'passage and find out? "

"No good," mutters he, audibly. "Didn't you hear the beastly place was full ? " Whereupon she subsides, as he does, with sullen resignation and scornful looks. There are still many hours of this forced companionship before them, and it is one of the hottest days of the year. All the elation with which they had set out seems to have evanesced, for how can they be free and jolly, joke and hugh, and play their game of three-handed cribbage, over which they have been enjoying themselves hugely so far, with this marplot sitting by? "Great Scott Why should we mind her though ? " Suddenly Mr. Triggs brisks up to make the above reflection. "After all she's doing us no harm, though she is a,.nuisance." .
He glances round. "She" has opened a book and is quietly reading. The child with round, amazed eyes, is solemnly inspecting everybody by turn.

If the mother, for she is certainly the mother, had been a pretty, fresh-faced, smiling creature, and, above all, if she had come without "the kid," Mr. George tells himself, he would have "done the civil," for he is 'all for making himself agreeable to the ladies, even when they incon- venience him and defraud him, as in the present instance. Possibly he would have gone further if properly responded to, and proposed turning their "three" game into a "four" one—but as it is he shrugs his shoulders: There is nothing attractive, certainly nothing responsive in the shrinking figure, with am 'grave- t viuraocd ootantont.rtoo, an a layr,Q. fixed steadily on the pages of an uninteresting volume. She is not good-looking according to his idea. No dash, no style about her. Widow, of course. Black and all that. No fun to be got out of such a party, and beastly hard luck it is that she should be thtre to choke up ,the carriage, and impose a restraint. "No, hang it; she shan't do that I" he Suddenly resolves. "I say, get out the cribbage," he commands aloud.

Of course, the ladies are delighted. .Their tongues are unloosed as if by Magic, the improvised board is brought forth, the cards are dealt, the pegs in their places. The little girl watches it all entranced. The mother never looks round ; seems to see nothing and bear nothing. By-and-bye they for- get her presence altogether. George's laugh resounds quite unrestrainedly. He claims a "fifteen two" from his sister and battles for it, she contending with equal ease and warmth. Mrs. George says "Sh—sh !" glancing towards their fellow-passengers. But, "Oh, come, never mind her. Let's be jolly," cries the husband, in a would-be aside. He is winning, and his fat face glistens with triumph and merriment. After all, he is having a good time, and what a glorious day it is, and what a rate they are spinning along at. He does, not mind the heat. It is nothing to the heat of their office,. he. avers.

He does not notice that the little girl has sunk back upon the cushions, having lost all interest in the game, and that her mother is bending over her, murmuring in her ear. Mrs. George does, however. "Good gracious I hope that nasty child is not going to be sick ! " "What ? " cries George, startled, and, without hesitation, he wheels round—for hitherto his back has been well turned on the interlopers—and takes obervations for himself.

Obviously there is discomfiture in the rival camp. The pale lady has flushed up and looks disturbed and anxious. The child leaning heavily against her is, on the other hand, as white as a sheet, and languidly indifferent to everything and everyone. For the first time the mother turns an inquiring, almost an appealing eye upon her fellow-travellers —upon two of them .at least, the two who are seated facing the engine. She and her little girl have back seats, and we all know what that means to some people. So far no one has thought-of it—but now? It is dreadful, but it is the only hope. for Dorothy. Dorothy's mother must ask those people. She does it with an effort only known to herself. "My little daughter is feeling the motion. It is very unfortunate, but if-7-if--" The Sp‘eaker stammers painfully_ They ean-see, -1/11,ulte, -bait ie what she wants, but no one is in a hurry to help her out.

"The child feeling sick, is she? Oh, well, you can change with her, Carrie." Mrs. George Triggs has' a sharp, high-pitched voice and calls a spade a spade, even when not as now annoyed, and only conceding in dread of a catastrophe. "Take care, don't upset the board. Clumsy," she subjoins, as the ether, not too willingly, makes as if to obey. It is all that Dorothy's mother can do to thank them, they look such dazgers at her and her offspring. And Dorothy does not want to move. Humphs a pettish shoulder and says : "No, let me alone," in the unmistakable accents of a spoilt child. "You will be all right if you sit on that side, dear."

Shame to say, the three who look on are almost pleased with the distress and perplexity and fruit- less efforts of their luckless fellow-passengers They have conceived a dislike to the mother apait from the grievance of her intrusion. She has sat so immovable hitherto, never looking round nor taking any interest in their games and their jokes; and now she must needs disturb everybody, in the very middle of a deal, too, because of her tiresome brat.

"I should take her out into the passage," says Mrs. Triggs, shortly. The words have barely crossed her lips ere Dorothy flies through the open door.. ...Never So long as she lives will,DorOthy's mother forget the-laugh which followed. She rose hastily. She felt as ii she could never return to her seat again.

"I can't tell you how grateful we are." Many hours ,have passed, and the train is now speeding its way through beautiful Scottish moor- lands, which the setting sun stlll lights up on every side, though it is past eight o'clock ere a halt is made at a small wayside station. "I am so glad we met von." continued the Speaker, and that you should be getting out herb too. You see, Dorothy calls you her friend. Rorothy's friend must come home with Dorothy,

div.head: MODERN FAMILY MEDICINE. Bile Beans are Unequalled.

div.head: SCIENCE NOTES AND NEWS,
div.p: SCIENCE NOTES AND NEWS,
THE EARTH'S SPEED OF REVOLUTION.

Everybody knows that the earth makes one complete revolution on its axis once in each twenty-four hours; but few, however, have any, idea of the high rate of speed at which such an immense ball must turn in order to ac- complish the feat of making one revolution in a day and a night. The earth, in making one complete revolution in the short space of twenty-four hours, must turn with a velocity al- most equal to that of a cannon-ball. In short, the rate of speed at the equator is exactly 1,507 ft. per second. This is equal to seventeen miles a minute.

div.head: ELECTRIC WIRE DANGERS.
div.p: ELECTRIC WIRE DANGERS.

Everyday experience proves that, of the fatalities from lightning or • from shocks due to accidental contact with 'live electric wires, by far' the greater number are to animals. The reason of this is that animals make far better contact with " earth " than men. For instance, an electrician wearing rubber • shoes can touch with perfect impunity a " live " high tension wiry. If he were barefooted and standing on iron it would be highly dangerous to touch even low tension wires. Again, when the hands are moist there is a much readier path for the elec- tric current, and hence the shock is very much greater than when the hands are dry.
FERTILISERS FROM EARTH'S INTERIOR.

Vesuvius proves to be a fertiliser factory of strenuous kind. Dr. Stoklasa, of Prague, calcu- lates that in one eruption the crater threw out upon the surrounding ground about 50,000,000 tons of mud, sand, ashes, lava, Sze- containing an average of 0•1 per cent. of nitrogen—the great fertilising principle. This product of 60,000 tons of nitrogenous fertiliser is more than is used in the whole of England. In addition the mountain has made enormous deposits of potassium phosphate and other fertilising salts, and the vapours constantly rising from the crater are laden with plant food.

div.head: HOW LONG IT TAKES TO THINK.
div.p: HOW LONG IT TAKES TO THINK.

According to Professor Helmholtz the whale probably feels a wound near its tail in , about one second, and requires another second to send back orders to the tail to defend itself. "The reason why the time occupied by this propaga- tion seems to us so infinitesimal lies in the fact that we are unable to perceive more quickly than our nervous system can act, and thus the intervals required for its operations appear to us imperceptibly small. Astronomers vary in their estimation of the moment at which a star crosses the web of their telescopes by more than a whole second, while the estimates of any indi- vidual taken by himself agree within one-tenth of a second if frequently repeated."

div.head: SIXTH SENSE IN BIRDS.
div.p: SIXTH SENSE IN BIRDS.

Although birds are not placed near the sum- mit line of evolution, their ability to fly gives them advantages over nearly all the mammalia. Their mysterious power of changing their polarity or weight, in order to dive in water or fly, has been often discussed, and the almost in- credible velocity of their motion when migrat- ing, sometimes amounting to four miles a minute for vast distances, has no parallel among other animals. A series of careful trials with carrier pigeons, reported from France, shows apparently without doubt their possession of a highly-developed sense of direction. In twenty minutes the first bird, despatched at 10 p.m., reached its roost, a distance of seventeen miles being traversed. Half of the number arrived before midnight, and the remainder followed in a 'few hours.

div.head: FINGERS AND TOES OF CRIMINALS.
div.p: FINGERS AND TOES OF CRIMINALS.

An Italian physician has studied the fingere and toes of 4,500 criminals, and finds a deficiency in the size or number of toes quite frequently among men. He has also observed that prehen- sile toes, marked by a wide space between the great toe and the second toe, is a condition quite common among criminals, also a webbed cori- dition of the toes, an approximation to the toe- less feet of some savages. He found the little toes rudimentary in many cases, shewing a ten- dency towards the four-toed animal foot. The most common of all the abnormalities was the webbed condition of the toes. These observa- tions agree with those made by various investi- gators, who have found other deformities exist- ing among the criminal classes, particularly mis- shapen heads, one-sided faces, mismated ears and eyes, &c. The criminal is a degenerate type.

BEWSEY-ROAD WESLEYAN CHURCH. Wesley Guild Festiyal. Sunday was the occasion of the Wesley Guildanniver- sary in connection with this Church. Both the morning and the evening services were conducted by the Rev. R. Bevan Shepherd, M.A. (Principal of the Frodsham Children's Home), who preached in the morning on the call of Gideon,as related in Judges vi.chapter and in the evening on "Temptation and its lessons," the sermon being based on the 12th verse of the first chapter of the Epistle of St. James. Dnring the evening aervice, which was very well-attended, T. H. Cowen's "The Promise of Life" was efficiently rendered by Miss Mason, a member of the church choir. On Monday evening the Rev. Bevan Shepherd delivered a highly interesting lecture entitled "An evening with Charles Kingsley.' Mr. J. E. Richardson presided over a good attendance. The LECTURER dealt more with the personality of Kingsley than with his actual work and the subject was most ably treated. Mr. Shepherd pointed out that in successful authorship and exceptional family felicities Kingsley passed his days honoured, appreciated and greatly beloved. His father was a man of culture, an artist, a linguist, a keen sportsman, and a lover of natural history. Like most West country men Kingsley appreciated the good fortune of being such all the days of his life. No-one perhaps, except R. D. Blackmore, had so vividly delineated and expressed the West county character and temperament and had translated the very atmosphere to his pages as Charles Kingsley. The lecturer then sketched Kingsley's career and dealt with some of his famous literary work. Whatever Charles Kingsley attempted, he said, was marked by extreme lucidity and intense earnestness. Whether it was the weaving of a West country romance or a dissertation on shells : discoursing on sanitary: reform or giving an exposition of chartism ; a description of Devonshire lanes or of Greek heroes ' • Kingsley made the subject clear to the very simplest of his readers and aroused enthusiasm in tbe most indifferent. The explanation was the man himself. He was simpler and clearer even than his own words—a brave, chivalrous, clever Englishman from head to heel.. ANOMALIES IN WINTER TEMPERATURE. The variations in temperature in different parts of the globe sometimes present curious anomalies. Thus it may happen that in mid- winter Greenland, in certain parts, may have a higher temperature than Southern Europe. Thus during eight consecutive days in November and December. 1875, it was warmer at Jakobshavn, in latitude 69cleg. 20min., than in Northern Italy, while Uperniyik. though in winter dark- ness, enjoyed a higher temperature than the South of France. 'These remarkable rises in temperature in Greenland are due, says the Globe, to warm winds, which blow down from the snow-covered interior, bringing on extensive thaws even in the middle of winter. Peary.ex- perienced such a wind in M'Cormick Bay, and on returning from an expedition found that the rain had fallen in torrents, melting a consider- able part of his snow house. This was in Febru- ary, and the thermometer rose to 41deg. Fahr. These warm winds are known as Fohn winds from the name given to winds producing a simi- lar effect in Switzerland. In this latter country the Fan is a warm dry wind, blowing down from the-snow-covered Upper Alps in autumn and winter, and suddenly melting off the snow. It has hence been callea the "snow-eater." A similar wind un the north-western part of the United States, blowing from the west into the !ulterior over Ithe Casca4e and Rocky Mountains, known as Ihe Chinook.

div.head: SLEEPING PLANTS.
div.p: SLEEPING PLANTS.

Plants sleep much the same as animals. Their sleep is quite real, and its reality can be shewn. Perhaps the best marked form of slumber in the vegetable world is that of the great winter rest. How does the long -winter rest of animals differ, after all, from the winter rest of the crocus or the hyacinth, which withdraw all the living material from their leaves in autumn and bury themselves inches deep in the soil in the shape of a bulb till FebruarNrains or April suns tempt leaves and flowers out again? The whole vast class of bulbous and tuberous plants, indeed— the lilies, orchids, daffodils, narcissi, tulips, squills, bluebells, and snowdrops—are they not just hibernating creatures, which retire under- ground in autumn with the slugs and the queen wasps, to reappear in spring about the same time with the return to upper air of the moles, the tortoises, and the fritillary butterflies?

div.head: OTOLITHS AND THEIR USE.
div.p: OTOLITHS AND THEIR USE.

It has been found by Ichthyologists that tho age of a fish may be read from its scales. These increase in size by annular growths, two rings being formed each year. The " Otoliths," or ear stones, which lie in two I sacs on either side of the base of the cranial cavity, afford another means of determination. Like the scales, the otoliths increase by two rings annually. Each spring, that is, from February to Jube, a white ring is formed, and each autumn, that is, from Jury to October, a black one. Thus the num- ber of either white or black rings in an otolith „gives the age of the fish in years. In the ease of flat-fish the latter method has been found more reliable, whereas in the case of the cod the scales give a better result. Although vary- ing much in size and shape in different species, the otoliths show a remarkable constancy in the same species. Hence they are of considerable value, in the diagnosis of a species.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
Primitive Methodist Centenary.

The concluding meeting in connection with the Primitive Methodist centenary celebrations at Legh- street Church was held in the choir vestry on Saturday evening. Mr. Cooper in a speech on "Our great need'' said that many men who had worked in the cause.of humanity, and had given the best of their lives in the service of their fellow-men, had probably gone down to their grave unsung and unhonourecl, and their names had passed into oblivion. Of all the great evils of to-day not one was irremediable, and their great need was to bring men and women who at present were living lives of degradation and drudgery, into whose lives not one gleam of sunshine came, and who knew nothing of the joys of life,into a cleaner atmosphere, into a realization of the truer and nobler life.

St. James' Church, Latchford The annual congregational tea meeting in connection with this church was held in the schoolroom on Mon- day evening and proved a great success. Over 400 persons sat down to tea,their wants being well attended to by the lady and gentlemen teachers of the school. After tea an excellent conjuring and ventriloquial entertainment was given by Mr. Harold Nimble. The Rev. H. B. FIRTH (vicar) then delivered an address. He said he was thankful to think they were still within the walls of a Chinch of England school. A great discussion had taken place throughout England on the subject of Church schools, but now that the Education Bill had been done away with, they were entering upon their work once more. They should, however, be prepared to make sacrifices for their church if called upon to do so. It was satisfactory to think that they had returned to St. James' Church after the alterations and decorations although the St. Hilda's Mission had served them well. He was glad to say that though a great deal of money had been spent upon those alterations, they were now only £3O in debt. (Applause). Last year when they were making great efforts for their church they were very liberally responded to. He would like to say a word as to the collections. The special appeal made upon them had been removed. It was perfectly impossible to work a large parish unless they had got the machinery. He was not going to ask them for a big sum, but if all would increase the amounts they gave on Sundays it would make a difference. ' (Applause.) A church like St. James', which conducted four services every Sunday, should at least take £4 in collections. If they had that then they would be able to better support their many organizations. They were very fertunate in having secured the Rev. Herbert Corsbie as their curate. Mr. Corabie was a man of experi- ence and ability' and it would be difficult to find one who would suit them better. (Applause). The Rev. H. CORSDIE said that when he had spoken of coming to Warrington be had been told," Well, you will find it very, outspoken." (Laughter.) He pro- posed a vote of thanks to those ladies who had so kindly presided at the tea-tables, and taken so much trouble to make the event the success it was. (Applause.) Mr. J. FARGHER seconded, and the motion was heartily agreed to. Dancing was afterwards indulged in, and was much enjoyed.

There are two pieces of "THE news from Johannesburg GOLD-REEF that should be considered CITY." together. One is to the

effect that a resolution has been passed calling upon the Government to despatch the unemployed to countries where work is available. The other is a report that the Boer leaders will support the retention of the Chinese if they are assured of another £10,000,000 for the purpose of re-establishing their farms and home- steads. This last is probably a falsehood,intended to influence the elections ; for it is particu- larly worth notice as an indication of the peculiar and unintellectual stubbornness of the minds which have been grouped round the Beit-Eckstein interests. This story, intended to discredit the Boer leaders, and set afloat, as it would appear, by supporters of Sir PERCY FITZPATRICK, assumes that if the Boers could be bought over to give their consent to the continued importation of Chinese the whole question would be disposed of. Men of the Sir PERCY FITZPATRICK class cannot be brought to understand that, whether or not the Boers can be bought over, the employment of Chinese in the Rand Mines under existing conditions, or any conditions remotely resembling them, must come to an end with the expiration of the present licences. That is something finally settled. We do not for a moment suppose that the Boers in the new Legislature will be bought over for .L 10,000,000 or for any sum which it is possible to name or imagine; but, in any case, the decision as to whether Chinese serfdom is to be continued in South Africa does not rest with them. If the Randlords were, outside of their own business, anything but very dull men, they would have long ago begun to understand that though, as CECIL RHODES said, they have made the British flag a commercial asset, that glorious emble m will again become, after a data that can now be fixed, a symbol of human freedom. We shall in the future be able to boast, as we have boasted in the past, that it cannot float over a slave.

The Randlords of Johannesburg are as deter- mined as the landlords of this country not to accept the decision of the last General Election. They believe that if they can tide things over for two or three years the Conservatives will again be in possession of power, and that they can then

have as many Chinese serfs as they like. This is another example of their impenetrableness to ideas that do not originate in the share market. Nothing could be much more certain than that no English Government, whatever its political complexion, will ever again sanction so shameful a document as the Chinese Ordinance. Even if Mr. BALFOUR and Mr. LYTTLETON were back again they dare not do it. It is not merely that a certain blood-curdling report stands in the way; but that the English people, now fully informed on the subject, are determined that there shall be no slavery in any part of the Empire and especially that there shall be no slavery under such non-human conditions as exist in the Transvaal. The unemployed men who are asking to be sent away from Johannesburg at the expense of the Government,are some of those who took Mr. LYTTELTON'S word RS to the extra number of white m3n that would be required in the mines when the Chinese were brought over. Many of them, it is probable, have wives and children somewhere, to whom they have promised to send money that never comes. In behalf of these wives and chil- dren the Poet LAUREATE writes no stirring ballads. Mr. RUDYARD KIPLING does not exhort us to 1" pay, pay, pay" for those who have been thrust into starvation by the mineowners, or to those who have gone to where nothing but hunger awaited them, because they believed Mr. LYTTEL. TON to mean what he said when he told the House of Commons that the importation of Chinese would proportionately increase the demand for white labour. Who would have dreamt, before the war, that" the gold-reef city" would by this time be confronted with such an unemployment problem as that which is briefly described in the latest news from Johannesburg?
There is to be a contest in
NVTIITECROSS Whitecross Ward after_ all,

VACANCY. for the Conservatives have plucked up courage to nominate a candidate in opposition to Mr. Joseph Hawthorn. As a rule we weicome contests for municipal honours—they indicate a healthy public spiric—but in this case it seems a waste of both energy and money. Tne seat can only be held for the balance of the late Councillor Brough's term of office, which would have expired in November, so that the winner of Monday's fight will have to come before the ele,?tors again in nine months. Possibly the Tories think this a good opportunity for attacking the Liberal stronghold. If they do they are likely to be soon undeceived, for Mr. Hawthorn is a popular man in the district and is expected to secure an easy victory. He should make an acquisition to the Town Council,which is not blessed with many young men of promise.

The battle on behalf of Sr. ararg's PARK. those who wish to preserve St. Elphin's Park as a "lung "for the east end of the town has nearly been won. At the private meeting of the General Purposes Committee on Monday evening the pro- posed purchase of the 14nd for £3,000 was warmly discussed and eventually rejected by 12 votes to 11. We understand that the issue will he raised again at the Council meeting on Tuesday evening and that there is every hope of carrying the scheme through. Public opinion in the neighbour- hood is almost unanimously in favour of the Cor- poration acquiring the land, and a memorial is being extensively signed by the inhabitants in order to strengthen the bands of Alderman Bennett and others who advocate the purchase. The objections on Monday were not so much against the proposal in itself and the outlay involved, but concerned matters of detail prin- cipally. Diffivilities such as arose could easily be smoothed over, and we hope the voting on Tuesday will show a substantial majority for the preservation of this green oasis in a desert of bricks, mortar, and tramways.

Thursday will rank as a THE INFIRMARY memorable day in the his- EXT EN SION. tory of Warrington for it witnessed the happy inauguration of one of the most deserving schemes ever undertaken in the town. Everything con- spired to make the ceremony of laying the foundation stone of the Infirmary extension a complete success. There was bright sunshine; Lord and Lady Lilford attended to take the chief part in the function; and a more representative gathering of townspeople has rarely been seen. The speeches were interesting and struck the right chord in as much as they expressed the desire which has united people of all classes in support of this great work—the desire to alleviate human pain and suffering. A few months hence and the extension will be an accomplished fact. It is the earnest desire of the committee that the building may be opened free from debt and we hope the generosity of Warringtonians will be equal to the occasion. Already the response has been beyond all praise, £ll,OOO of the £15,000 required having been raised. The urgency of the extension has often been emphasised in these columns and those who subscribe may rest assured that their donations could not be devoted to a more useful and necessitous cause.

div.p: NOTES AND NOTIONS.

After speaking at Stockton Heath on Thursday, Mr. A. J. King, M.P., motored home to Bollington near Macclesfield, a distance of about 30 miles. tre The Marconi Wireless Telegraph Co, Limited, report that the wireless telegraph traffic for Marconi- fitted ships for 1906 is 1,261,000 words sent and received, as against 783,050 words of 1905. * *

Are not the suffragists, in honour—to their previous victims—bound to declare war on all the 005,000 members of the Labour party? Even they might quail from such a task.—" Morning Post." * * * Sankey Brook has come under notice again and the Public Analyst has supplied a report to the members of the Sanitary Committee. Of late, the brook hag been specially obnoxious, and the process of purifica- tion seems to make very Jittle, headway.

-* ,„ Great interest will be taken by Warringtonians in the eisteddfod to be held at Preston to-day. Two local choirs—the Warrington Male Voice Choir and the Apollo Prize Choir—have entered and we hope that one of them will be fortunate enough to carry off the prize

The suggestion is made in" London Opinion," that if the Salvation Army is really in earnest in wishing to save people from committing suicide it should do away with its bands. We should like to add " and street-corner singing too," though we have much admiration for the work the Army does for the " sub- merged tenth." . .

* * * A sub-committee consisting of Councillors Ellison, Evans, and Benson, has been appointed to consider and report on all available places in and near tha Borough suitable for open-air bathing. We would like to suggest the new street behind Bridge-street. There is a fine open space there which is of little practical use at present.* * * Mark Twain once made an amusing comment on a white marble bust which he saw in the library of a friend. It was the bust of a young woman curling her hair, a very graceful modern work. Mark Twain looked at it and said, "That isn't true to nature." "Why not? " was the reply. "Because she hasn't her mouth full of hairpins." * * * Only one of Dr. Macnamara's many telegrams of congratulations has baffled him. It reads: Llongyfarchiadan Gwresocaf, and comes from Swansea. Perhaps some of our local N.U.T. members could help their fellow-teacher to decipher the message.

Mr. A. H. Crosfield, M.P., will address a mass meeting of his constituents in Parr Hall on Monday the 18th instant, and will probably be supported by Mr. W. E. Harvey, M.P., this week's victor in North- East Derbyshire. At the present time Mr. Crosfield is staying at Cannes, recruiting his health for the ensuing Parliamentary session.

* * * The Chester Consistory Court has just granted a faculty to the vicar of All Saint3', Thelwall, to erect a tablet to record the building of the town and fortress of Thelwall by King Edward the Elder in 922 and the Coronation of King Edward VII. in 1902. The commemoration of the deeds of the earlier and " elder " Edward is a bit late in the day,—but better late than never ! Perhaps some future Edward will renew the glories of the ancient city of Thelwall. 0 0 _

If I were a man I would invariably before going to a theatre take a ten-mile walk, smoke a couple of strong cigars, and drink three bottles of lemonade or soda-water. Then when I had comfortably settled into my stall I should sit there contented as a log, and should not be impelled by an ever-recurring insatiable thirst, by an uncontrollable muscular restlessness, or by a fever for nicotine, to tread upon the toes, dis- arrange the hair, and exasperate the tempers of the hapless women who should chance to be along the route of my perpetual goings out and comings in.— ARIBELLA KENEALY in " London Opinion."

Mr. Henry Roberts appe-ared. before the General Purposes Committee on Monday to request on behalf of the Soldiers' Memorial Committee that the cost of constructing the foundation and erecting the memorial should be borne by the Corporation. The sum involved was about £175, and the Committee declined to entertain the request, one member remarking somewhat unkindly that the Memorial Committee wanted to take all the honour, and the Corporation to find the money. It would be far better that the money should be voluntarily contributed. There is no sound justification for making it a charge upon the rates.

Thursday night's Liberal meeting at Stockton Heath was the ninth Mr. A. J. King, M.P. has addressed in about a fortnight. Every part Of the constituency has been visited, and the Member has been very warmly received everywhere. The spirit of Toryism in Cheshire seems to be crushed flat, for Mr. King has not encountered any opposition at his meetings. In addition to the Member, Mr. Joseph Smith, the Liberal agent for the Division, has also had a busy time. All the nine meetings have been arranged by him from headquarters at Knutsford, with assistance from the local committees, and they have all been remarkably enthusiastic and unanimous con- sidering that this is a slack time politically.

** * - Mr. W. E. Harvey, M.P., who has fought and won the Liberal and Labour battle in North-East Derby- shire under great difficulties, has found his way from the pit to one of the leading positions in the Derby- shire Miners' Association. He was born fifty-five years ago at Hasland, near Chesterfield. in his youth lie was compelled to face many difficulties. His father died when he was an infant, and before be reached the age of ten he was working in the mine twelve hours daily for the modest sum of tenpence. In winter he saw daylight only on Sundays. When he was eighteen he, with Mr. James Haslam, now M.P. for Chesterfield, worked strenuously to organize the miners of Derbyshire, and in 1881 the present associa- tion was formed

Mr. Haslam left the pit soon after the inauguration of the association, he having been appointed its secre- tary, and soon afterwards he was joined by Mr. Harvey as assistant secretary. The two have ever since worked in company to build up the Miners' Union, with the result that to-day it has a membership of 26,000, with funds amounting to £200,000. Mr Harvey had several opportunities to enter Parliament, but he preferred to wait for an opening in his native county. He is a member of the Chesterfield Town Council, and was recently appointed a Justice of the Peace for Derbyshire, * * *

There is more litigati-on with the Ship Canal Company possible. The Rivers Committee recom- mends the presenting of a petition to Parliament against the Manchester Ship Canal (Various Powers) Bill, 1907. The Company proposes to put down plant at Eastham and Latchford capable of raising five million cubic feet of water per 24 hours, to purchase lands at Arpley and raise them to the level of the railway embankment, and to pump water from the lower reaches of the canal into the higher reaches for lockage purposes. The Warrington Corporation is concerned as to the effect tliese pumping operations may have on the waters of the Mersey and Bollin which flow into the length above Latchford, and pre- cautions are being taken in the interests of the town and the traders on the river.

div.head: LOCAL NEWS.
div.p: LOCAL NEWS.

Coming Events. The annual ball in connection with the Warrington Market Tenant's Association will be held in the Parr Hall, on February 14th. The annual sale of work in connection with Cockhedge Mission will be held on Thursday and Friday; to be opened on Thursday by Mr. Rigby Armitage, and on Friday by Mrs. Rylands (Massey Hall). An exceptionally attractive entertainment is promised at the Parr Hall on Thursday evening next when the second annual concert in conneetion with the Secondary School will be held. An excellent programme has been arranged, including vocal and instrumental selections, costume and action songs, and scenes from Shakespeare's" A midsummer night's dream." There will be a chorus and orchestra of 200 performers. The proceeds will be devoted to the School Athletic Club. The annual ball in connection with the Warrington Corps of the St. John Ambulance Brigade will be held at the Conservative Club Assembly Rooms on Thursday evening. Mr. A.Starkey's band will be in attendance. We would remind our readers that the members of the Warrington Musical Society will give their final cencert of the season in the Parr Hall on Saturday evening next the 9th inst., when the proceeds will be given to the Infirmary Extensicn Fund. The pro- gramme will be one of exceptional interest, and will be provided entirely by members of the society. It will include the Market Chorus from " Masaniello," the " Miserere " scene from "II Trovatore," " Liberty" (E. Faning), "Hail, bright abode" (" Tannhauser "), part songs, &c., solos by members of the society, orchestral selections from " lolanthe suite, " Rural scenes," intermezzo from " Cavalleria Rusticana." Popular prices have been arranged and reserve seats may be booked at Mr. R. H. Pearson's, Bridge-street. To-night's penny popular concert at Bold-street school will include a new series of living pictures, songs by Miss Cox, Miss Carrie Hastings, and Mr. L. Aukland and a recitation by Miss Maddock. MYSTERY OF A COTTAGE FIRE. A maiden lady named Sarah Joynson, aged sixty-two, Who lived alone in a small cottage off Lowland-road, Runcorn, was discovered dead under extraordinary circumstances on Tuesday. She had not been seen luring the morning, and the house was entered. Miss oYnson was lying dead on the hearth with her face badly scorched, while the cottage had evidently had a narrow escape of destruction by fire. A broken lamp Was on the floor, and a sofa and sewing machine were Practically consumed, and all the other furniture and Pictures were much charred. It is thought the old lady had overturned the lamp and had fallen down and been suffocated. She was partly dressed, but her 010 thing Was not burnt.
