DEATH OF AN OLD RESIDENT.

Many Earlestown people will hear with regret of the death of Mr. Barr, of Burn Bank, Cross-lane, who died his residence on Monday afternoon after a short illness. lie was well known in the town, having been connected with the London and North-Western Waggon Works for bout 4O years. lie was 66 years of age.

After a repast provided by the hostess, Mrs. Chapman. the President, Mr. Chapman, presented the prizes won atinu,lng the season. VIADUCT WARD. At a meeting of the Earlestown and Newton Conser- "ytlve Working Men's Association, held at the Conserva- tive Club, Earle-street, Earlestown, last Thursday night lithe President introduced Mr. A. Tunstall as the candi- jae chosen for the Viaduct Ward. Mr. Tunstall, in a rief speech, said that if he was returned he would prove to them that the confidence of the voters in him was not misplaced. CRUELTY TO A HORSE.—AN AMBULANCE CASE. At the Liverpool City Police Coirt, last Thursday orning, when David *Forshaw, of Fairclough-street, ar.lestown, was summoned for having worked a horse whilst in an unfit condition. Mr. Duder prosecuted for the police, and called evidence to the effect that .on January Ist a constable on duty in Upper Parliament. Street stopped the defendant, who was driving a horse attached to an ambulance. The animal was in an exhausted condition, and almost unable to stand. The officer questioned the defendant, who stated that he had that morning travelled eighteen Miles --from Earlestown to Liverpool—with the ambul- ance, for the purpose of conveying a female patient and two of her friends from the Royal Southern Hospital back to Earlestown. The ()Meer had the horse removed to a stable in the neighbourhood, and the occupants of the vehicle were sent down in a cab to Lime-street Station, returning to Earlestown by train. The horse was examined by an officer of the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals. It was found to be suffering from acute debility, and was quite unfit to travel, either with or Without a vehicle. The journey of eighteen miles from Earlestown to Liverpool must have caused the animal -considerable pain.—It was explained that the ambulance belonged to the Earlestown District Council, and the defendant had horsed it for this special journey. He was a carrier in a small way of business, and was in Poor circumstances. The Earlestown Police reported that the woman, whom defendant had arranged to con- Vey home from the Liverpool hospital, was not able to Pay the ordinary car hire, and it was an act of charity on the defendant' part.—The defendant said the terms '913011 which he had been engaged were ss. for each lciurneY.—The Chaiaman observed that if it had not been for the Earlestown police report they would have dpalt with the defendant very severely. Under the circumstances he must pay a fine of les. with ss. 6d. cost.

ALLEGED MARKET THEFTS AT ST. HELENS. At St. Helens Police Court, on Tuesday, a woman named Louisa Davies, of 9, Sutton Heath-road, should 'have. appeared before the magistrates on a charge of stealing articles from stalls in the market. The Chief Constable said that since she was locked up she had been taken ill, and he had sent for a doctor, and he would ask for a remand until Saturday. Police- constable Ramsden arrested the woman in the market the previous night, after seeinq her take an article from t? stall, and on her house being searched a number fif articles were found which were presumed to have been stolen. The magistrates granted a remand.

Lloyd George and he never knew a President of the Board of Trade who in that short time had exerted so much influence to the advantage of the country. The Liberal party were able at the last election to have a clear fight between THE FORCES OF RE-ACTION AND PROGRESS.

At almost every election during the last 40 years, they had been dominated by some question which was not really a question between re-action and progress. The Eastern Question, Home Rule,South Africa and so on had always diverted public attention from the real distinctions and the real difference between progression and retrogression. He was inclined to think that this country, when it had a fair chance would always be Liberal and Radical—(applause)--though they might have times of aberration and be drawn away from various quarters and for various reasons. He thought he could say without hesitation that the aspirations, hopes and desires which actuated the Liberal party and this Federation at the last election were shared to the full by every memaer of his Majesty's Government. (Applause.) Lord Durham once uttered these fine words : "I will freely own to you that lam one of those who see with regret every hour that passes over the existence of unreformed and acknowledged abuses." He believed it was the policy of the Government to fulfil those desires and aspirations. However good the output of last Session might have been, whatever might be the out- put in successive sessions, he did not think the Govern- ought to be judged until their policy and their time of , office was complete. He asked that there should be no 1 hasty judgment on the part of the Liberal and Radical party until the Government had fulfilled the task they were sent to perform. The question of administration I was almost as important as that of legislation. If they looked at the Foreign Office he thought even the Con- i servatives admitted that Sir Edward Grey—(applause) had carried out a good and satisfactory and peaceful 1 foreign policy. With regard to the Colonial Office, 1 South Africe was handed over to Lord Elgin in a state of absolute chaos, although the Conservative party ; fought the previous election on the basis that they were the only people who could bring peace and a settlement to that land. The Liberal Government desired to hold an even hand between the two races and the various interests involved there and they were ' determined as far as THE CONSTITUTION OF THE TRSNSVAAL was concerned, that it should be neither jerry-built nor , jerry-mandered. (Applause.) With regard to the administration in the various general offices, the chilling atmosphere of the last twenty years was passing away and it was felt that the administration of the great offices such as the Admiralty, War Office, and Post Office was to be placed on a more national humane and satis- factory basis than it had been for some time.(Applause) They felt that there was a policy in view, for the first time for twenty years, of economy and reform in regard , to rates and taxation. They had seen that the trade of the country had on the whole been satisfactory and 1 whilst he never said that was brought about by the • existence or action of any particular Government,it was an awkward fact for their Protectionist friends that the exports, upon which they always founded their argu- ments, had gone up by leaps and bounds. It was very seldom now that we heard of Protection, and it was not the merits of Protection which were being talked about as the Protectionists were quarrelling over Mr. Balfour's body. (Laughter.) As they were aware, for two or three years past, no-one, including Mr. Balfour himself, knew what Mr. Balfour's views were in regard to Pro- tection—(aughter)--and he was afraid that in some future years the Protectionists might find that Ur. Balfour was a Free Trader (Applause). At all events Ur. Balfour would see which side was coming out on top and his open mind would then be made up. (Applause). With regard to the future there was one measure which was pressing—the question of electoralreform. That was a question in which they were very much interested. They could not believe under the present circumstances that the country was on a democratic basis or as democratic as it ought to be as a constitutional ' monarchy because whilst many oi them were in favour of

div.head: BIG LIBERAL MEETING LAST NIGHT.
div.p: BIG LIBERAL MEETING LAST NIGHT.
Visit of the Right Hon. Sydney Buxton, M.P. and Mr. Hilaire Bolin M.P.

The Parr Hall was the scene last evening of one of the most interesting and successful Liberal meetings ever held in the town. The proceedings had been arranged by the Lancashire and Cheshire Young British Liberals' Association and the Warrington Junior Liberal Association and were rendered memor- able by the visit of a Cabinet Minister in the person of the Right Hon. Sydney Buxton, M.P., Post- master-General. Another of the principal speakers was Mr. Hilaire Belloc, M.P., one of the most promising of our Liberal politicians. The admirable arrangements which had been made were a tribute to the vitality and usefulness of the Junior Liberal organizations which have made such great headway of late. There was a large attend- ance and the utmost enthusiasm prevailecl.Prior to the meeting an organ recital was given by Mr,W.H.Payton Mr. C. E. Parker, President of the Warrington Liberal Association, presided and was supported on the plat- form by the leading Liberals of the town and district as well as delegates from the Lancashire and Cheshire British Young Liberals' Association. Letters of regret at being unable to be present were received from Mr. A. J. King, M.P., Mr. W. J. Crossley, M.P., Sir ,Charles Schwann, M.P., Mr. T. G Horridge, M.P., Mr. A. H. Scott, M.P., Mr. Pollard, M.P., Mr. J. M. Astbury, M.P., Mr. Herbert Paul, M.P., Major Seely, M.P., and Mr. Edwin Hamar (Liberal candidate for Blackburn). LETTER FROM MR. CROSFIELD MP _ , . .

Mr. A. 11. Crosfield, M.P„ wrote : —" I am writing to ask you to tell Mr. Buxton how very deeply dis- appointed I am to miss hearing the speech he is going to deliver in Warrington. We are all of us —especi- ally the Junior Liberals—greatly honoured by the visit of this distinguished Statesman and Member of the Government, and I cannot well explain to you in a letter how vexed and grieved I feel at my enforced absence from Warringtin at this time. As explained in our correspondence a few weeks since, I was unable during the Autumn recess to take a single week's holiday free from business and politics, and as my health was not too satisfactory last year, Sir VictJr Horsley ordered me to go South for along and complete rest in the middle of the Autumn Session. I did not choose to leave London with so many important political riaestions on the tapis then, but I feel I must obey Horsley's instructions and remain quietly here to accumulate some reserve of health and strength before Parliament re-opens on the 12th of next month."

div.head: MR. A. J. KING, M.P., AT SIMON HEATH.
div.p: MR. A. J. KING, M.P., AT SIMON HEATH.
ENTHUSIASTIC MEETING.-THE SESSION REVIEWED.
Mr. H. Vivian, M.P., and Trades Disp3tes:Bill.

Mr. A. J. King, NLP. for the Kautsford paid a visit to his constituents in Stockton Heath on Thursday evening and addressed a crowded meeting in the Hall Card. The proceedings were of an enthusiastic description and there was every evidence that the Liberal feeling in the district has not suffered a re-action or been allowed to die down since the General Election. Mr. H. Roberts presided and in addition to the member there were present on the platform :—Mr. H. Vivian, M.P. (Birkenhead), Messrs. C. Jackson- Holmes, C. E. Parker, J. 114-mgland, E. Lloyd-Jones and J. Smith (Knutsford).
MR. H. ROBERTS AND THE EDUCATION BILL.

Mr. H. Roberts said that during the past year a great deal of legislation had taken place. With regard to the very great and burning question of Education, if the action of the House of Lords in rejecting that measure on the prompting of a Tory minority, carried home to the convictions of earnest people the fact that an hereditary house of legislators supported by the Bench of Bishops—who had for a long time been distinct enemies to the freedom of the people—if they realized that that condition of things was an •abominable anomaly and ought not to exist, then the misfortune of the loss for the time being of the education measure would not be without good results. (Applause.)

div.head: SPEECH BY MR. KING.
div.p: SPEECH BY MR. KING.

Mr. A:4. King, who was received with applause, moved "that this meeting records its confidence in the work of the Government and the House of Commons during the last session, strongly protests against the obstruction of the House of Lords and assures ! the Prime Minister of its support in his deternaination that the will of the people must be made to prevail." (Applause). Lord Newton recently said "that the present House of Cornmons,was different from its predecessors, as it was composed for the most part of ardent democrates who meant business and who were thoroughly in earnest." (Applause). If they wanted confirmatory evidence of that he would refer them to the record of work during the past session. In spite of the opposition of the House of Lords no less than 56 measures had been placed on the statute book in 190 a figure which he thought compared very favourably 1, with the 23 measures passed by the Tory administration ! in their last year of office. Many of the measures had been hanging about the House of Commons for many years and the Government could have made the same excuse as the Tory Government and pleaded that they had not time to deal with them but instead of that they tackled them with energy and determination and said "If we , cannot get them through in the day time we will sit through the night." In the House of Commons at the present time there were many men who were specialists in yarious departments of social reform. They had Mr. Vivian—(applause)—who,with others,was deeply inter- ested in co-operation and the housing of the people, and much practical work was being done in the direction of founding better houses for the people of the country. He never before saw agriculture So well represented, from the point of view of the tenant farmer and the agricultural labourer. All the various sections of ardent reformers were actuated by one common motive—to see something done and done quickly to raise the standard of comfort of the masses—and all minor differences were sunk and they were united on any programme of reform which the Government might introduce. (Hear, hear.) Amongst the Bills which had been passed they had a little measure of which he had very great hopes that it would produce a condition of things more in keeping with their ideas of justice.—

_ _ THE QUA.LIFIC.A.TION OP JUSTICES BILL which abolished property qualification for county magistrates. He knew that on that question he was on delicate ground but he recognized that the present state of things was intolerable. The county Benches for the past 20 years had been packed with men of one political opinion. They believed that not only should the Benches be very largely leavened by men of other political opinions but by representatives of the various classes of society. (Applause.) They in Cheshire were sorry that up to the present there had not in that county been any practical result of the measure but he would ask them to have a little patience. He for one had faith in the Lord Chancellor—than whom there was no better Radical in the country—and believed that he would readjust the political bias on county Benches and satisfy the most exacting of those who wished to see reform in that direction. (Elear, hear.) There had been three or four measures passed for the benefit of agriculture and especially in the interests of the tenant farmer, and he hoped that next session they would have a measure specially dealing with the grievances of the agricultural labourer. The farm labourer's position at the present time was one of the most hopeless of any class of people in the country, and he hoped the Government would pass a measure which would provide on a large scale not only good houses for the labourer but houses w;th land attached in the form of small holdings so that he might eke out his wages by cultivating his own land and also be induced to remain on the soil. (Applause.) There were two other very important measures which I had been crying out for a long time and for the passing of which the Tories had never found time. One of these gave the farmer the right to claim compensa- tion from the owner of dogs which worried his sheep. Then there was the'Crown Lands Act. As they knew there were in various parts of the country certain lands belonging nominally to the Crown, but managed by the Government. This land had now been banded over to the Board of Agriculture,and it was the intention of the Minister of Agriculture when the leases of crown land fell in, to let the land in small holdings. Formerly the land had been let in the form of very large farms, but I in the future, he hoped, they would find a larger,happier I and more prosperous population on the land at present I occupied by a few only. (Applause.) Another measure,the I Agricultural Holdings Act made arbitration between I land owner and tenant much simpler and also provided that a tenant farmer could claim damages from the landowner, as compensation for loss suffered by the deprivation of winged game. The Act also gave the 1 tenant farmer the right to what crops he would I grow.

THE WORKNIENS COMPENSATION ACT had included some 6,000,0110 people in the benefits of compensation who had never been included before. He had hears it urged that it tvas a great hardship to include domestic servants. The insurance however was but 3s. per annum per servant, and he did not think that burden could be regarded as intolerable. (Applause.) The Merchants Shipping Bill had been waiting for many years for someone with the courage and ability to carry it through the House of Commons. By that Bill many of the conditions in the lives of sailors had been materially improved. A compulsory scale of food had been fixed for foreign-going ships, and in all hew ships the air space in the sailors'quarters had to be increased. Then again the regulations in respect to the load line which formerly applied only to English ships, had been extenddd to foreign ships entering or leaving a British port, and by this means a grievance long felt by the British owners had been removed. (Applause.) They all knew of the suffering caused amongst children by endeavouring to force into their brains education which , they were not physically fit to receive. The great I difficulty was to find a remedy and the Education (feed- ing of children) Bill was mostly of a tentative character. By it the authorities could make provision, in the shape of room, for voluntary effort. Tn some extreme cases the authorities were empowered to spend money to the extent of a half-penny rate but in that case they were required to collect the money from the parents to whom the advance was made if they were capable of repaying it. Wisely as the Liberal Government had acted in its legislature it had, he maintained, acted with equal wisdom in its administration. (Applause.) Mr. Lloyd George had assisted chemical manufacturers by the removal of the tax on alcohol used for manufactur- ing purposes and he was also taking up the question of

Bad legs and diseased ankles are hard to cure once they have been wrongly treated and neglected. The flesh may ulcerate from sheer weakness, brought on (especially in the case of women) by excessive standing or kneeling, while in many cases the tiniest scratch has spread into some torturing humour or those terrible, weakening wounds that eat deep into the flesh. Zam-Buk has achieved unparalleled success in the treatment of bad legs, and sufferers should try this unique skin-cure without delay. Mr. George Sinclair, of 1, Assembly-street, Dumfries, said to a" Courier and Herald " reporter : "Being employed in a shop I shave to be on my feet most of the day and every day. About eight months ago I got a little injury to my right ankle while play- ing football, a piece of skin being torn off. Within a week the wound had got aboutaquarter of an inch deep, the skin round about was discoloured, and the flesh In the hole very red and inflamed. Watery matter began to discharge, and the ' itchy ' feeling became positive pain. I tried *sing a chemist's ointment for nedrly four weeks, but the wound got wider and I went to the Infirmary. I attended twice and sometimes three times a week to have it dressed and bandaged. I was unlucky enough to meet with another accident, being hurt on the inside of the same ankle by knOcking it against the sharp eige of a box in the shop. The result was that a similar wound appeared there, and it also was treated at the infirmary. The pain was bad before, but after the second wound came my sufferings were almost unbearable. At last I began to use Zam-Buk, and was astonished that the first application gave me so much relief. I applied the balm twice a day, and noticed how the wounds got less daily, how the ugly raw colour disappeared, and the discharge ceased. Finally scars formed, which soon fell off, leav- ing a new healty skin and by the end of a fortnight both wounds were healed."
Zam-Buk is Nature's own skin-cure. Every home needs a box of this unique and useful balm.

div.head: ST. PAUL'S CHURCH TEA PARTY
div.p: ST. PAUL'S CHURCH TEA PARTY
Presentation to the Vicar.

The annual congregational gathering in connection with St. Paul's Church is always looked forward to with pleasure. and the success which attended the tea party and entertainment held in the Parr Hall on Monday evening was highly gratifying. Admirable arrange- ments had been made for the function Mr. H. B. Houghton discharging the secretarial duties. About 300 sat down to tea, ladies of the congregation presid- ing at the tables. The concert which followed was exceedingly enjoyable. Miss Florence E. Brown, who possesses a sweet soprano voice of good range, very effectively sang" April Morn " and " The nightingale's trill." For a feeling interpretation of " Annie Laurie" Miss Mabel Henshall was heartily encored and responded with a charming" Japanese love song." Later she delighted the audience with "The little Irish girl." Mr. J. Forrester sang "Four jolly sailormen " and "Father O'Flynn " with fine spirit and he, too, was recalled. A pleasing feature was the duet "The spider and the fly" by Miss Brown and Mr. Forrester. Two mandoline solos were creditably played by Miss M. Stanley. The male members of the choir acquitted themselves well in the part songs "Sailors chorus" and. " When evening's twilight" and were cordially encored. There was no lack of the humorous element, Mr. J. Macdermott, of Liverpool, creating great merriment with his songs "A song without a name" and "How the winds blow." Master Dick Lawton also proved a ' popular favourite,his singing of" Killicrankie" and the narration of several anecdotes pleasing the audience immensely. Mr. E. Wilkes was an able accompanist. During the interval there were some interesting speeches and the assembly also had the pleasure of witnessing a presentation to the Vicar (Rev. W. Bracecamp). The Mayor (Alderman Smethurst) pre- sided and was supported by the church officers. The Vicar expressed regret at:the absence of Miss Westwell, through illness, and of the Rev. E. Peters, the newly- appointed curate, owing to bereavement. The Mavort pointed out that they had had many reasons for thankfulness at St. Paul's Church during the year and they were all particularly pleased that the Vicar declined the offer of a living at Sheffield and decieed to continue his good work amongst them. Mr. Bracecamp was one of those ministers who hit straight from the shoulder but they appreciated him all the more for it, and they were thankful to see the church so well filled every Sunday evening. The Mayor made special reference to the building of a new vestry and expressed the hope that the debt on the restoration fund would soon be cleared off. (Applause). Mr. J. RIGBY (people's warden) said the finances of the church were in a satisfactory condition. The offertories kept up to the usual standard and when appeals were made for special objects the congregation always responded liberally. During the year they had raised £27 ss. for the Infirmary, £36 10s. 9d. for the Vicar's Easter offering, £4O at the re-opening services, £4O at the harvest festival, and £l3 78. 9d., at the laying of the foundation stone of the new vestry. The total amount received up-to-date for the restoration fund was £695 2s. 9d. but so many improvements had been made that there was a debt of £4OO. He hoped, -however, that they would soon be able to clear that off (Applause). • Mr. J. H. SMETHURST, after expressing tho pride of the parishioners of St. Paul's at having a member of their congregation elected to the Mayoralty, urged the congregation to support the clergy fund. He was glad that the penny bank continued to flourish, there being considerably over 1,000 depositors. The congregation had endeavoured to loyally support Mr. Bracecamp and the result was to be seen in the satisfactory state of the church. They were all delighted that he decided not to go to Sheffield but to remain at St. Paul's. The officers of the church felt they would like to make some little recognition of the Vicar's work and they had subscribed to present him with an illuminated address which they hoped he would accept in the same spirit it which it was given. (Applause). Mr. SMETHURST then handed to the Vicar a handsome framed address which read as follows :—January 28th, 1907. St. Paul's Church, Warrington. We, the under- signed officers of the above Chnrch,desire to place upon record our appreciation of your work in this parish during the past four years. We recognise that it is in a great measure due to your efforts that the Church, of which we are all so proud, has flourished both spiritu- ally and4ataterially in that time. More especially we desire thank you for the spirit of self-denial which promptei your recent refusal of the offer of a living which was more advantageous from a pecuniary stand- point. We pray that God may bless yourself, wife, and children in the future, and assure you of our continued support." The VICAR briefly returned thanks. He said he was sorry they had looked at I. is action with regard to the Sheffield offer in the-light they had done, because every Engislaman ought to do his duty. He knew it had been said by outsiders that he bad some private reason for refusing the living, but he said honestly and sincerely

div.head: WARRINGTON
div.p: WARRINGTON

Personal. Mr. J. Kenworthy, of Warrington, has been elected a member of the Executive of the, Liverpoal District Lay Preachers' Association of the Lancashire Con- gregational Union. ' A PUBLIC BENEFIT, UNDER THE CLOCK FOR BEST BOOTS DI LANCASHIRE.—Advt. Popular Penny Concert. . There was again a crowded attendance at the weekly concert on Saturday evening, and an excellent pro- gramme was submitted. Songs were given by Misses Gertrude Gilding (Liverpool) and Lily Mason, and Mr. H. Plumpton, whilst Miss Mellor was warmly applauded for several recitations. The humour was provided by Mr. Barker, of Manchester, and Mr. E. J. Burgess. The accompanists were Ifessrs. G. W. Weaver and H. Mellor. The proceeds were devoted to the Kingston Earthquake Distress Fund. Boarding a Moving Train. William Powell, nurseryman, Fearnhead, Warring- ton, was charged at the Warrington Police Court, on Monday, with entering and leaving a moving train at ithe Central Station. On Wednesday, the 9th inst., defendant rushed on to the platform and boarded an express train to Manchester whilst it was in motion. On ascertaining that it did not stop at Padgate he jumped off, and had it not been for the timely appear- ance of a porter he might have fallen between the carriage and the platform. 4 fine of 10s. including costs was imposed. " HERALD " KITCHEN RANGES and " Peveril " Fire Grates are hard to beat.—Sole agent, J. S. GARLAND, 51 to 55, Bridge st., Warrington.—Advt. Coroner and Unprotected Fires. Mr. S. Brighouse held an inquest at Warrington on Monday on Edna Crompton Fryer, the four-year old daughter of Alfred Fryer, engine driver, 137, Orford- lane, who died from burning injuries sustained on January 9th. The child was left in the kitchen with three other children whilst her mother was upstairs. A wax taper was procured, and whilst running into the yard with it lighted deceased's muslin pinaforte caught fire, and she was terribly burnt about the body, suc- cumbing in the Infirmary on Friday night last.—The Coroner remarked that since October 2nd. he had held eighteen inquests. The Legislature Aught to step in and make it an offence for parents to-leave children in a house were there was an unprotected fire. Until the Legislature stepped in so long would this lament- able ; oss of life continue,—A verdict of" Accidental death" was returned. PUBLIC BENEFIT.—UNDER THE CLOCK FOR BEST BOOTS IN LANCASHIRE.—Advt. P.S.A.Gatherings. An open meeting of the Warrington P.S.A. Society was held in the Co-operative Hall, Cairo-street on Sunday, Councillor Steel presiding over a large attendance. An address was delivered by Mr. Jones (president) on the evils of gambling and drinking. Miss V. Brown sang "The volunteer organist" and "The gift," and Mr. Herbert Barnes, "Nearer, my God, to Thee," the efforts of bath being warmly applauded. At a meeting of the Wycliffe Society Mr. Joseph 0 wen presided over a fair attendance. Mr. Barbery, of Oldham. gave an address on "Throw- ing out the life line." He referred to some sights he had seen in connection with wrecks on the Cornish coast, and in including the work of throwing out the life line. Christ was the great life line for the storms and distresses of the human soul. He was the sure anchor and refuge for the weary and sad. He was sure all present had a great regard for the Christ, the Saviour of the world. The hymn "Throw out the life line " was heartily sung. Mr. Payton presided at organ. Mr. Joseph Hawthorn also took part in the meeting. LADIES' BEST GLACE BOOTS AND SHOES, UNDER THE CLOCK, BRIDGE-STREET.—Adtv. Shorthand Writers' Association. The weekly meeting of this association was held at the Winmarleigh Cafe on Wednesday night, a fair number of members being present. After speed practice (which is an imp )rtant feature of the associa- tion's work) the Hon. Secretary (Mr. Joseph Marsh) gave a short, but instructive lecture on a phono- graphic principle. The latter portion of the evening was occupied by the reading, by 'Mr. A. N. Legge, of a Federation paper entitled "The Reading of Biography." The educational benefits to be derived from a course of biographical reading were referred , to, and the writer was of opinion that a much more , correct impression of a personage historically famous,' or the true significance and.-result of a series of notable events, was to be obtained from biograpey than from an ordinary history. Another useful purpose served by the reading of biography was that it opened up one's sphere of inquiry. One read so much of an' occurrence, and became so interested, that, as a result, one's thirst for knowledge was considerably, increased. The Lecturer hoped that those who did not read much would participate more in what he termed a "delightful nnd instructive occupation," and would include in their reading that of biography. He con- eluded by asking his bearers to rembember the oft- quoted lines : "Lives of all great men remind us vie can make our lives sublime." The meeting closed with the usual vote of thanks. WOOD CHIMNEY PIECES, Fire Grates and Tiles unrivalled seletion, inspection invited.—J. S. GARLAND, Builders' Ironmonger, &c., 51 to 55, Bridge st., Warrington.—Advt. Death of Mr. J. T. Foard. . Many of our readers will regret to hear of the death of Ur. James Thomas Foard, barrister-at-law, which 'took place on Saturday at his residence, Lancaster- road, Birkdale, in his seventy-sixth year. With his headquarters in Liverpool Mr. Foard was for many years a very familiar figure among barristers practis- ing in the Northern Circuit generally. In connection with the courts held in St. George's Hall, Liverpool, especially -- including the assizes, the city sessions, &c. —he was long honourably known, though of later , years he was scarcely so much in evidence as when lin full vigour of his manhood. For many years he held a position as revising barrister for one of the districts of South-West Lancashire which included Warrington, and his invariable cou:tesy to those who appeared before him earned for. him the warmest esteem. Of .rather a retiring disposition, though of refined testes, his inclinations led him, for the pur- poses of recreation, to association with such institu- tions as the Literary and Philosophical Society of Liverpool, a society founded in 1812, and bearing on its list of presidents such names as Sir Edward Russell, and the Rev. G. H. Rendall, M.A.,Litt.D. (ex-Principal of the Liverpool University College), now head master of Charterhouse School, &c. As president of the Literary and Philosophical Society, elected not many months ago, Mr. Foard may be said to have died in i harness. It is interesting to note that Mr. Foard read , a paper on " Shakespeare " before the Warrington ; Literary and Philosophical Society last session and I previously he had lectured on " Sir Walter Raleigh" Ibefore the Warrington Society. By his many friends in the Warrington district he will be much missed. UNDER THE CLOCK for Good BOOTS. Advt.— Assessment Committee. A meeting of the Assessment Committee of the Warrington Union was held at the Workhouse yester- day morning under the presidency of Mr. A. J.Jolley. There were also present : —Messrs. William Houghton, ' G. Mather, T. H. Ashcroft, S. Davies, and A. Brooks, 1 with Mr. J. C. Sutton (clerk), Mr. W. H. Woodcock I (assistant overseer for Warrington), Mr. Houghton , I (assistant overseer for Newton), Mr. Joseph Dickinson ' 1 (assistant overseer for Haydock), and Mr. Joseph I Smith (assistant overseer for Great Sankey). Mr. IT. S. Steel, solicitor, appealed on . behalf !of Mr. W. C. Brooks against the assessment of the Raven Hotel, Fennell-street, which stood at £95 gross and £BO 103. rateable. He pointed out that several tenants had been unable to make the house pay and 'Messrs. Greenall had reduced the rent from £BO to Ito £6O. Mr. Brooke felt that the present assessment was altogether 'too high, that he could not make the lbusiness pay, and the house was not worth the present ! rental. On a previous occasion the assessment had I been reduced by £5. The taking down of houses, I the closing of one works and the reduction of the num- ber of employees at another had all tended to decrease 'the business done at the hotel. —The committee decided to reduce the assessment by £lO, imaking it £B5 gross and £72 10s. rateable.—The Valuer (Mr. R. A. R. Meacock) reported with regard to Messrs. Guest's tannery that having regard to the compactness of the tannery and the terms under Which it was let, he was of opinion that the present assess- ment gross £360 and rateable £2BB was about a fair one. He had also made a valuation of the South Lancashire Tramway Company's line in Haydock and begged to submit :—Gross. £136, rateable £6l 10s. as the present value of the undertaking. This equalled about £5O per mile rateable value. As this hereditament was in a somewhat unsettled condition, he would suggest that the committee had the assess- ment adjusted annually for a time.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
RUGBY FOOTBALL.
[By " Ovalist."]

There seas very little Rugby football in either 'Lancashire or_Yorkshire on Saturday, owing to the firm hold of the ground that Jack Frost had got. Neither of the Warrington teams was engaged, Ind only four fixtures in the Northern League came off. Warrington should have made the journey to Oldham, and there was hope of the match being played up to Friday night, but the final snap of frost got through the straw covering and caused an abandonment of the game at the last minute. This will be a severe loss to the Oldham Club, which would probably have had a 10,000 gate for such an important fixture. ' Of the matches that were played, Halifax did the best performance in thrashing Bradford on their own ground. Leeds beat Brought >n Rangers—who have done very badly in Yorkshire this season—while Wigan and Hull had easy victories over Hull Kingston Rovers and Leigh respectively.
The League Table up-to-date is as follows : For Aga. Per-

The positions of the four leading clubs remain unaltered, but Oldham are such close rivals of War- rington that the game at Watersheddings means a good deal to both clubs. If Warrington can win there they will practically only have Runcorn to struggle with, and there is the West Lancashire Cup at stake between the two also. Wigan have the highest scoring aggregate, but when Warrington have finished with Liverpool City and some of the other clubs due at Wilderspool they should not be far from leading the way to all in the accumulation of points.

That there will be more changes in the Northern Union rules at the next annual meeting is pretty certain. The thirteen-a-side game seems to be in favour both in Lancashire and 'Yorkshire but there is considerable opposition to the present lax knock-on rule which seems to put a premium on bad play, and leads to trickery when near the line. Then the absurd constitution of the League is generally con- demned, with its unreal competition and its puzzling percentages, and we shall probably see a reversion to the ordinary League with first alai second divisions.

Two league matches have been played during the week, Dewsbury beating Hunslet by 7 points to 6, and Huddersfield running up 63 points to nil against poor Liverpool, whose adverse total now stands at 844 points.

Warrington are due at Widnes to-day and as the points are doubly valuable to the wirepullers they will probably seoure them. I notice that the same team as last week has been chosen despite criticism. This is only natural. The Committee can rise superior to the newspaper critic at any time—except when the annual meeting is drawing near. However the side should be good enough for Widnes, though it 'will want strengthening to oppose Oldham. As it stands to-day it is: Berry, full back; Hockenhall,lsherwood, Dickenson, and Brooks, threequarters ; Lees and Jenkins, half backs ; Preston, Thomas, Heath, Harmer, Naylor, and Shugars, forwards.
The Oldham match has been arranged for Monday afternoon, and no doubt a few ardent Warringtonians will make the journey.

The " A "team should have Wigan Highfield as visitors to-day, and as they have memories of an' unpleasant reverse to wipe out there should be some fun. A strong team is available,for both Ike Taylor and Matt Lambert are down again. Teams : Knight, full back ; Taylor, Cartwright, Jones and Jordan, threequarters ; Lambert and Kay, half backs ; Belton, Swift, Jolley, Forster, Holbrook and Hewitt, forwards.

"Jack Fish is looking rare and well again, and he tells me he hopes to turn out at Huddersfield on Saturday next and at Halifax on Shrove Tuesday. Jy the way the story is told that a black cat strolled into the Halifax pavilion fourteen weeks ago, and remained there. The team has since won every match and puss is being taken care of. Fish says he is going to take his prize coursing dog to catch tit° Halifax cat and break the spell.

The League matches for to-day4iVe•r'— Widnes v. Warrington. Halifax v. Leeds. Hunslet v. Huddersfield. Wigan v. Bradford. Hull Kingston Rovers v. Batley. Hull v. Runcorn. Wakefield v. Oldham. Broughton Rangers v. St. Helens. Salford v. Liverpool City. Swinton v. Barrow. Leigh v. Rochdale Hornets..

div.head: DEATH AND FUNERAL OF MR. THOMAS HALL.
div.p: DEATH AND FUNERAL OF MR. THOMAS HALL.

On Saturday last the remains of the late Mr. Thomas Hall, who for some years past had resided at Statham, Lymm, but who was formerly a well-known tradesman in Warrington, were quietly laid to rest in the graveyard at Hill Cliffe, in the presence of a few relatives and friends including :—Mr. E. Jafnes Hall (son), Mr. Joseph Hall (brothers Rev. Henry Briggs, Todmorden (son-in-law), Mr. dames • Robinson Hall (grand- son), Messrs. Thomas and Alfred Al br nson, George Hall, S. Fernley and F. Rice (nephews), Messrs. C. and J. Marsh (brother-in-law), and Mr. T. J. Lee who carried out the funeral arrange- ments. There were also present at the graveside : Mr. Henry Greenall, Mr. Henry Roberts, Mr. W. Fletcher, Mr. J. Longland, Mr. W. H. J. Jenkins and the members of the Executive of the Warrington District of the Independent Order of Rechabites who had attended in response to the invitation of the District-Chief Ruler, Bro. R. Harrison, in order that they might pay their last tribute of respect to their deceased brother who had been identified with the Order for a period of over half a century and fulfilled with honour every position in the District Council, being at the,tinie of his death one of its trustees. The service was conducted by the Rev. A. J. W. Back, of whose church at Lymm iVlt.Hall had been for a number of years a member and an elder. Previous to Mr. Hall retiring from business and taking up his -abode at Statham, he had a long and happy connection with the Baptist Church at Golborne- I street, indeed it was owing to Mr. Hall's efforts sup- ported by a few other friends that this Church was instituted in the year 1869, first meeting in an iron building in Rylands-street, afterwards purchasing the present valuable premises in Golborne-street. During 1 the course of the etening service on Sunday last, an appropriate and touching reference was made by the , Church Secretary to the passing away of Mr. Hall. In a few well chosen words he referred to Mr. Hall's long and faithful connection with the church, at the close of which the cengrertbn gave expression to their respect by passing a vote of condolence with the widow and relatives, and standing during the playing of the Dead I •March.—At the annual meeting of the Church held on Thursday evening, it was decided that steps be taken to , place in the Church some permanent memorial to Mr.l Hill's memory, and a small committee was appointed with that object in view.

Viscount Coke, Lord Lieutenant of Norfolk, will unveil on Wednesday next a bust of Visoount Nelson, presented to Burnham Thorpe, the birthplace of the great Admiral, by the London Society of East Anglians and erected in the church. The Bishop of Thetford will deliver an oration on Nelson at the ceremony.

div.head: CAIRO-STREET ANNIVERSARY.
div.p: CAIRO-STREET ANNIVERSARY.

Special services were held at Cairn-street Unitarian Church on Sunday, in celebration of the anniversary. Large congregations assembled both morning and even- ing and addresses by the Rev. W. Lawrence Schroeder, of Sale, were listened to with marked attention. The annual congregational tea was held in the schools on Monday eveuing,and, as in past years, proved a great success. About 120 ladies and gentlemen sat down to an exqplient tea and this number was considerably ' augmeftd for the meeting which was subsequently • held. Mr. J. Hill presided. Mr. F. W. PURSE gave a report upon the work of the , Sunday school and allied institutions. In the Sunday • school whilst the number of scholars had slightly , decreased the average attendance had been maintained. Mr. F. MONKS gave some very pleasant reminiscences of Cairo-street Chapel, with special reference to the successful and useful ministry of the Rev. P. Carpenter. I Mrs. Booth and Mr. Whitehouse contributed songs in a very able manner, and the choir were heard to advan- tap in their rendering of two carols. The Rev. W. LAWRENCE SCHROEDER in the course • of an address on "The new theology," said it was i undignified for Unitariang to hurry the new theology I into the acceptance of a name which its believers did I not want. They might call it by a different name, but ! in essence it was that which made for religion in the ! deepest sense. The religion behind these men was I making for the wider position. God had moved many Unitarians in a certain direction of theological expression, and might they not trust Him to move even independently of Unitarian influences in the same direc- tion among their orthodox brethren? Theologies might separate but the Master's Christ-like spirit brought men and women into an organio unity. • (Applause.) i The Rev. C. HARVEY COOK delivered an address on • the work of the church during the past year, and the meeting terminated with a vote of thanks to Mr. Hill for presiding .

div.head: 1 THE BREATH OF THE PINE FOREST.
div.p: 1 THE BREATH OF THE PINE FOREST.
The Right Way and the Wrong Way of Treating Coughs. and Colds.

The advent of Peps, the pleasant pine-air treatment for throat, lung and chest diseases, has superseded old- fashioned treatment by medicines through the stomach as completely as modern methods in medicine have superseded the bleeding-cup. Medicines to benefit the lungs and bronchial tubes should obviously reach the affected parts direst. Peps convey the pleasant balsamic essenoes of the rich pine woods straight to the seat of the trouble.
Lungs. to Stomach,

A medicine for the chest and lungs is all wrong if it has to be merely swallowed into the stomach, which has no direct connection with the .lungs. You cannot swallow anything into ycur lungs. Old-time chest, lung and cough medicines are just as wrong-headed in effect as they are in composition. They are usually heavily drugged with opium, chloral, morphia, or some other narcotic,or else loaded with bromides or other sedatives. By dosing the nerves they often stop a cough, N 5 ithout removing the cause. It is dangerous to merely stop a cough, for coughing is Nature's way of expelling phlegm, disease germs, and other obstructions from the throat, lungs and chest. If you stop the cough before its work is done,by putting your nerves to sleep, your chest, throat and lungs get clogged up with impurities. Peps cure coughs and colds by making the cough easy, natural, and painless, and by destroying disease germs. . You simply take a little Pep from its silver paper wrap- ping and let it dissolve on the tongue,or crush it between the teeth. This releases the pine essences imprisoned in the tablet, and immediately the nasal cavities, the throat, the lungs, and the bronchial tubes are filled with the healing breath of the rich pine woods. Breathing becomes easy and natural when the breath is impregnated with the rich balsamic pine air from Peps; phlegm is loosened, and brings out with it all the dust and germs inhaled from polluted air; coughing is eased and allayed, and the clogged up air passages are cleared. , Be on your guard against substitutes and imitations. See that the registered name—Peps—is on every box you buy: There is nothing "just as good "as Peps. div.p: MY DEAR NIECES AND NEPHEWS,— • Owing to a very naughty cold naving taken complete possession of me, I am afraid you must not expect a very bright letter from me this week. It is rather inconvenient, and I dare say you all know what it feels like to have a jolly bad cold, and an invitation to two or three parties at one and the same time. What can be more distressing than to know that a lot of dear friends are revelling in the glories of "Postman's Knock" and "Musical Chairs," whilst we o-urselves are bolstered up in front of a roaring fire, enveloped in several chest protectors, a dressing-gown, a couple of travelling rugs, and a pair of carpet slippers? But, away with melancholy; let me feast my eyes in imagination upon the mighty bundle of pretty picture postcards, which I anticipate with next week's post-bag. I can see myself roaring at the little twiddley bite that will be inecuibed upon each—the funnier the better, my dear children. Make your dear old Uncle scream, till his withered old sides seem to crack—for he is a firm believer in the old adage that a Rood laugh is better than doctor's medi- cine. I hope you -;Eire all going to try for the lovely prize that lam giving, each week, for the best card sent•in. Have you any objection to my putting the usual weekly question to you? "How did YOU spend Christmas-day?" and requesting you to send me the reply in writing, so that I may see who is most entitled to the "How I spent Christmas-day" Prize. I received two more conthibutions for that prize this week, but Ern still requiring a few more; so, as the showman said, "Hurry up, ladies and gentle- men" UNCLE NED,

div.head: WELCOME TO
div.p: WELCOME TO
Kate Johnson.
REPLIES TO CONTRIBUTORS.
IDA B.—l am afraid, Ida
that your coutribu-

tion. is a little beyond the "Corner" style. I shall be glad to receive some simple ditty, which will appeal to the very young members. OLIVE K.—Thanks for letter. I think you have received it by this time. Was glad to hear from you. DORIS T.—l have received your letter, but I am sorry I cannot undertake to accept any- thing which is to be continued. If you for- ward me the complete tale, and it is not too long, I will see what. I oars do. It is very good of you to try and help the "Corner."
THE POOR OLD SOLDIER.

An old soldier, with a wooden leg, came into a village, and was suddenly taken ill, and was obliged to seek the i3helter of a barn. Little Agatha, the daughter of a poor basket-maker, had great compassion for the sick man, and visited him every day, and made him a present of some money. But one day the honest soldier was much distressed, and said, "Dear child, as I have learnt to-day that thy parents are poor, pray tell me candidly how you get so much money? Because I would rather starve than re- ceive a single farthing which you could not give with a good conscience." "Oh," said Agatha; "do not ,be anxious on that account; the monek is lawfully obtained. I go through a road where there are many wild strawberries, so I gather my little basket full every time, sell them in town, and receive a halfpenny. My parents know the whole matter very well, and have nothing to say against it. They often say that there are many people podrer than we are, and so we must do them as much good as our circumstances will permit." Some time after, a distinguished officer, who wore many orders, was passing through the village, and drew up his magnificent carriage before the old inn,when he heard of the sick soldier, and went to visit .him. The old soldier immediately told of his benefactress. "What I" exclaimed the officer, " has a poor child done so much for you? Then I, your old General, can be allowed to do nothing less. I shall make arrangements at once that they provide for you the best at the inn." He did so. Then he went to the- cottage .of little Agatha. "Good child," he said, "your benevolence has made my heart warm. You have given the old soldier many coppers; here you have, instead of them, as many gold ones." I remain, your loving nephew,
HARRY M. DIIXBURY.

Dear 'Uncle Ned,—Many thanks for the box of chocolates; they are beauliful. 'I hope you will like this postcard. I am trying to win one of Newball and Mason's free footballs, as you advised us to do in the paper.
ARTHUR FEARN.

Dear Uncle Ned,—l was very pleased to see my letter in print. I am sending you a piece of poetry, and hope to see this in print also. I should very much like to have a bottle of Mason's Extract, if you have any left. I think this i 5 all now.
From your lotgg Niece, Dm Bow.

fear Uncle Ned,—l should very much like to become a member of the "Children's Corner." Having read it for some time, I have at last summoned up courage to write to you. I am 13 years old, and am in the Eighth Standard. I am sending you a short story, called :

div.head: "TAKEN AT HIS WORD."
div.p: "TAKEN AT HIS WORD."

Some years ago, in Russia, a man wiN con- demned to be put to death. When the moment came for the sentence to be carried out, the Czar, who presided over the execution, asked him if there was any one petition that he could grant him. All that the condemned man asked for was a glass of water. They went and got him a tumbler of water, but his hand trembled so that he could not get it to his mouth. The Czar said to him, "Your life is safe until you drink that water." He took the Czar at his word, and dashed the water to the ground. They could not gather it up, and so he saved his life. •
From your loving Niece, KATE JOHNSON.

Dear Uncle Ned,—l am sending you a short story, which I hope to see in print, as I have not been successful in seeing my last two letters in print. I should like very much to have one of your bottles of Mason's Extract of Herbs. Wishing you a prosperous New Year, - I remain, your loving Niece,
GWENDOLINE KIVELL.
"THE TERRIBLE DISCOVERY."
He was a dear little tot of four, with long, flaxen curls. It was tea-time.

' He had five pieces of bread and butter, four buns, sixteen fancy biscuits, and a jumble. Suddenly the little fellow leant back in his chair, and burst out crying. His doting parents rushed to his side. "My angel, what is the matter ?" " 800-hoo, I's lost my appetite."

div.head: WHEN EVENING BRINGS ITS HOME.
div.p: WHEN EVENING BRINGS ITS HOME.

Forgot the trials of the day, The toil, the grief, the care, All seemed to fade at sunset ray, The world grow bright and fair. And yet the shadow deeper falls, And weary wanderers roam; But through the gloom a loved voice calls, When evening brings us home.

Dear Uncle Ned,—l am writing to thank you for the bottle of Mason's Extract of Herbs, which I received on Saturday. I am sending you a few riddles, as I hear you want some. The more you take away, the larger it gets, What is it?—Answer: A hole.

I am a piece of gold, my house is made of I crystal, no door nor windows have I, yet people come in and steal me.—Answer: An egg. . Why is it dangerous to sleep in a train?— Answer: Because the train runs over sleepers. . White as snow, but it is not snow; green as grass, but it is not grass; red as fire, but it is rot fire; black as ink, buti it is not ink. What is it 7—Answer: A blackberry. Hoping to see this in print, I remain, your loving Niece, OLIVE KIVELL. '
"THE LONDON THIEF."

A farmer and his wife once went to visit London for the first time. The farmer, dressed in his best clothes, went to look at the pictures in the National Gallery. They had no sooner entered the door when a man came out and said visitors were not allowed to go in with their boots on, because they spoilt the polished floor. They soon removed their boots. The man said he would mind them until they came back. When the farmer went in he was surprised to see the other men with their boots on, and he quickly returned to the door to look for the man who had his boots, and he soon found that he was a thief.
GWENDOLINE KIVELL.
I wonder how many little C.C.L. heads the following cap fits! Dear Uncle Ned,—l am glad I am in your League, and I am sending you this piece ,31 poetry, which I hope you will like. It is called:
DAINTY. She couldn't eat this, and she wouldn't touch
that, She screamed at the sight of a morsel of fat; She always declared that she couldn't bear meat, In fact, there was nothing she fancied to eat. Her breakfast was "horrid," and so was her '
dinner; No wonder each day she grew thinner and thinner.
There were coaxings and scoldings from mother
and nurse, , But daily this dainty young lady got worse, Until she could scarce take a sip or a bite, Declaring she really had no appetite; And she grew such a scarecrow, so pale silo so
- thin, That the family doctor at last was called in.
"Tut., tutl " said the doctor, and knitted his
brow. "Such nonsense as this we can never allow! Insist, my dear madam, and make her obey, And eat what is given her every day. Take heed lest your dear little daughter you
spoil, And--dose' her with plenty of cod-liver oil" I EVA SYLVESTER.

div.head: FREE CHURCHES.
div.p: THE FREE CHURCHES.
(By Our London Correspondent.)
THE " NEW THEOLOGY."

Among the Free Churches the one matter of interest above all others just now is the "New Theology "which has been propounded by the Rev'. R. J. Campbell, of the City Temple. Apart from the personality round whom the controversy has raged, it must be confessed that of recent years there has been considerable shifting of the foundations of belief, not only among the Free Churches, but in all the communions. The effects- of the Higher Criticism, together with the progress of scientific and historical study, has under- mined the old ideas of the verbal inspiration of the Scriptures, and, of course, anyone of influence and authority—especially if he be of the magnetic influence which Mr. Campbell undoubtedly pcssessee—is eagerly listened to if he offers a new systematic re-statement of theological beliefs. That being so, it. is easy to understand the commotion Mr. Campbell's crusade has caused. As to the exact effect of his utterances it is difficult to. say. One word of caution is necessary—practically the whole controversy rages round words which axe only intelligible to the trained mind, and into which any of the disputants can put almost any meaning they choose. The doctrine of the Divine. "immanence," for instance, is orthodox or unorthodox, just according to what meaning you attach to it.

div.head: BOLD ASSERTION.
div.p: A BOLD ASSERTION.

In one stat3ment Mr. Campbell was clear when he laid down that "to say Jesus Christ had not a'human father is untrue." On this, ()Onion is overwhelmingly against Mr. Camp- bell; anyone may say that the doctrine of the Virgin Birth is "improbable," but to say it is "untrue" is to make a statement as pre- sumptuous as it is unprovable. In pulpits all over the land there have been repudiations of this. At one well-known suburban church of my acquaintance the congregation—emi- nently respectable and stolid—could not re- frain from breaking out into applause when their pastor condemned this particular utter- ance.
NATIONAL COUNCIL MEETINGS

The programme of the meetings of the National :Free Church Council at Leeds next month is practically completed. I understand that it is still possible for a few Personal Members' tickets to be granted. The conditions are: (1) Membership of an Evangelical Free Church, (2) Payment of ss.
NATIONAL COUNCIL AND EDUCATION.

People' I find; are wondering what the National Free Church Council will have to say on education when they meet at Leeds next month. No doubt the- assembled Free Churches will speak with no uncertain voice oa the matter. For, the preserit' it is felt that the position rests with the Government. The National Free Church Council has carried on the most vigorous agitation ever since the introduction of the Education Act of 1902. But now it is more a constitutional, issue than a question of education; the larger issue takes in the smaller. If the Government are not able to find some way to make their proposals effec- tive they will lose all reputation, and might as well resign at once. But the feeling among Nonconformists is that the Government can and will find a way. So we wait in expecta- tion.

div.head: PASSIVE lIESISTANCI
div.p: PASSIVE lIESISTANCI

As was to be expected, Passiveßesistance has shown increased vitality since the wrecking of tho Education —Rill by the Lords, and the movement is extending to many wno -previutiNiy- did not feel justified in resorting to this form of protest. Up to the end of last year there were some 80,000 summonses and 191 persons had been imprisoned, some many times. A great National Passive Resistance Day has been arranged at Whitefields on February 5. It will commence at 12 o'clock noon with sermon by Dr. Campbell Morgan; at 2.30 there will be a Prayer Meeting, pre- sided over by Dr. Bendel Harris; at 3.30 there will be a Gonference, opened by Mr. P. W. Wilson, M.P., on , "Pas- sive Resistance from the Constitutional View," and Rev. J. Hirst Hollowell, "From the Nonconformist View." After tea in Top- lady Hall, there will be a public demonstration at 7.30 under the Chairmanship of Dr. Clif- ford. The speakers are to include,Dr. Rendel Harris, Rev. C. Silvester Horne, M.A., Mr. G. Hay Morgan, M.P., Mr George M.P., and others.
NEW TEMPERANCE LEGISLATION

It is expected that Temperdnce will be one of the matters to early occupy the attention of the Government during the coming Session. In view of this the Free Church Chi o for February gives a well-informed article by Mr. E. C. Rawlings, J.P., on "The New Government :Temperance Legislation." Mr. Rawlings deals with reduction of licences, compensation, time limit, Sunday closing, etc. All friends of temperance reform are anxiously awaiting the proposals of the Government, and it is to be earnestly hoped that some measure will be introduced that will unite all sections of temperance reformers. Even the brewers are persuaded that some legislative reform is necessary to and the present chaotic condition of the licensing laws, and certainly the Chris- tian conscience of the-land demaiids some legislation which will make it easier for the tempted to do right and harder for wrong to prevail. 'MR. MEYER'S NEW WORK.

Next month The Rev. F. B. Meyer termi- nates his connection with Christ. Church, Westminster-bridge-road, and at the Leeds Meeting he will be formally set apart for the special visitation of Councils and Churches under the auspices of the National Council. This visitation will extend over several days at each place,- and will touch the whole of Free Church life and method. Mr. Moyer's unique gifts in this direction are widely re- cognised, and his robust evangelism is bound to produce the best result:. Immediately after the March meetings Mr. Meyer will go to Germany and—America, and on his .return will commence his special missions.. All ar- rangements for Mr. Meyer's services are being carried out by Rev. Thomas Law at head- quarters, Memorial Hall, London, E.C., to whom all applications should be sent. Already IFge number of such applications have been received.

div.head: INFIRMARY.
div.p: THE INFIRMARY.

LAYING THE FOUNDATION STONE OF THE EXTENSION. Lord Lilford's Yisit. Thursday marked an epoch in the history of the Warrington Infirmary, as it witnessed the laying of the foundation stone of the extension on the site adjoining the existing premises. The scheme which involves an expenditure of £A5,000, has been rendered imperative by the ever-increasing demands upon the accommodation of the institution, and an appeal to the public for assistance has met with a generous response. Up to the present £ll,OOO has been raised, and it is hoped, and confidently expected, that before the new building is opened the whole of the cost will have been met. Thursday's ceremony, which was performed by Lord Lilford, was the occasion of a ' striking demonstration of interest and enthusiasm, the proceedings being watched by a large crowd. Lord and Lady -Lilford arrived at the Town Hall shortly after noon, and were there welcomed by the • Mayor and Mayoress (Aid. and Mrs. Smethurst), and a, number of the leading townsmen. Here a pretty inci- dent occurred, as prior to the departure for Kendrick- street, Mrs. Pickmere, on behalf of the Infirmary Exten- sion Commiitee, presented Lady Lilford with a beautiful shower bouquet of pink carnations and lilies of the ; valley. The proceedings at the reception were of a purely informal character, and prompt to time the party left the Town Hall, and headed by Crostleld's Band, proceeded to the site of the extension via Sankey-street and Legh-street. Here a large crowd had assembled, and an animated spectacle was presented. For the time being the ugliness of the scaffold poles was hidden beneath a covering of brightly-coloured bunting, whilst flags both large and small fluttered gaily in the sunshine and breeze. A large platform had been constructed, and to martial strains from the band Lord and Lady Lilford and party took up their stations upon it. Amongst those present were the Mayor and Mayoress The Rev. H. V. and Mrs. Pigot, Mr. and Mrs. W. Peter Rylands, Canon and Mrs. F. W. Willis, Canon Penrhyn. Miss Willis, Alderman Bennett, Councillors Burton, Sankey and Benson, Mr. \V. Garnett, Mr. and Mrs. P. C. Garnett, Mr. and Mrs. R. Pierpoint, Colonel and Mrs. Edelsten, Mr. and Mrs. John Fairhurst, Mr. E. Wallington Mr. H. R. d'a Willis, Mr. and and Mrs. J. H. Thompson, Mr. Vere B. Davies, Mr. G. P. Miln, Rev. P. Whittle, Mr. E. Garland, Mrs. Geddes, Rev. J. Roche, Mrs. Milling, Mr. L. Atkinson, Miss Boyle,Miss , Wilson, Mr.S. Taylor Mr. NlcQuire, Alr.J. A. McGregor, Rev. and Mrs. E. C. E. Carleton, Dr. Hodgkinson, Rev. C. Harvey Cook, Miss B. Dutton, Mr. R. T. Fairclough, Rev. J. Manning, Mr. L. Bennett, Captain Crosfield Mr. Lister, and Mrs. Lord. At the outset Mr. W. PETER 'MAUDE, in a brief speech pointed out that the Infirmary was almost 100 years old. it derived its origin in 1810 when a few prominent citizens of Warrington joined together and formed a dispensary,which had since performed a useful work in the town. In 1877 it was moved to the present buildings. Is had been a matter of sincere and deep regret and anxiety to the Board of Management for some years past that the Infirmary bad been absolutely and hopelessly insufficient to meet the growing demands of the town and after careful and anxious consideration it was decided to put in hand the scheme for the exten- sion in the hope that the result of the movement would be the proper satisfaction of the infirmary needs in Warrington for many years to come. (Applause). A prayer of dedication was then offered by the Rector, and an appropriate passage from the scriptures red by the Rev, J. Yonge. A cavity in the stone was next uncovered and in this Lady Lilford deposited a vessel containing coins of the realm, current issues of the the local Press and of the British Medical Journal and thelnfirmary report for 190 G. Lord LILFORD was the recipient of a silver trowel and an ebony mallet from the hands of the Rev. EL V. Pigot and Mr. W. P. Rylands, and the stone having been placed in positisn he declare it to be well and truly laid. In a brief speech he expressed the real pleasure it gave him to receive the invitation to come to Warrington and inaugurate that work, because, amongst other reasons, an undertaking of that description was entirely free from any share in the controversies which occa- sionally and so unhappily divided the people. No better object could engage their attention than the development and progress of an institution devoted solely and entirely to the alleviation and cure of human suffering. In supporting such an institution they were performing not merely a local but a national duty because it was a well-known fact that the enormous development and advancement of medical science in latter years was largely,if not entirely due to the work done and the discoveries made in such institutions. He knew Lancashire people quite well enough to know that once they were persuaded of the goodness and usefulness of a thing they were second to no people in the world in their loyal support and he sincerely trusted that from that stone would rise a building worthy of the town and one which would be of permanent and being good to the town and neighbour- hood. (Applause). The trowel presented by the Committee to Lord Lilford is from the designs of Mr. G. S. Gilbert, and, I together with the mallet, has been obtained through Messrs. Eustance aed Co., Ltd., of Warrington. The trowel, which is of solid silver, with ebony shaft, has been specially designed for this occasion. The chief characters of the trowel are the emblematical figures forming the handle, of a woman and child representing Sympathy. On the blade is emblazoned, in enamels, the coat of arms of Lord Lilford, surrounded by a wreath of olive leaves. Worked into the shoulders of the blade are two cherub heads. The wording on the trowel and mallet is as follows :—" Presented to tho Right Hon. Baron Lord Lilford on the occasion of his laying the Foundation Stone of the Warrington Infimary Extension. 31st January, 1907." The MAYOR proposed a vote of thanks to Lord and Lady Lilford for their presence. Mr. GEORGE DAKIN seconded. The Rev. P. WirmLE supported the motion. He wished to publicly express the gratitude of the section of the town which he had the honour to represent for the great boon an institution like the Infirmary was to them. As they were aware Catholics were not a wealthy body. The bulk of them were workingmen and women and they would appreciate what a god-send it was to them to know that in the case of serious accident ett h they could go to an institution like the Infirmary where they would be attended to by skilful doctors and most devoted nurses. At the conclusion of the ceremony, there was a public luncheon in the new lecture room at the Volunteer Quarters. The Rev. H. V. Pigot, chairman of the Board of Management, presided over a large company. The catering was in the hinds of the Winmarleigh Cafe Co. and gave satisfaction. After luncheon a number of toasts were honoured. The Rev. H. V. PIGOT explained that he occupied the position in the unavoidable absence of Mr. J. Charlton Parr, the president of the institution who took a great interest in the work. They also regretted the absence of Mr. and Mrs. Long and he need not remind the gathering what a splendid start Mr. Long gave to the fund by subscribing 1,0004 Applame.)The Misses Wilson-Patten who had already subsclibed 100 guineas each, had taken the opportunity of forwarding another live guineas each. Mr. W. H. Blackly, Mr. J. J. Bleckly, and Mr. Coxon were also unable to be present and Mr. David Garnett forwarded a donation of .£25. The loyal toasts were enthusiastically honoured on the proposition of the CHAIRMAN. " BISHOP AND CLBRGY OF THE DIOCESE AND MINISTERS OF ALL DENOMINATIONS." Mr. ROBERT PIERPOINT proposed this toast, and said the ceremony therbad just witnessed was one of those ever-recurring examples in this good old town of how the ministers of Christ worked together, no matter to what sect they belonged. Their one object was to do what they could in their time to promote the welfare of their fellow men and women. This was an age of entente cordiale. They started that entente cordiale among the religious bodies many years ago, and he trusted it would last for ever. (Applause.) The RECTOR, in responding, said he was specially delighted by the recognition of God in that day's cere- mony, and by the co-operation and kindly feeling which existed between the clergy and ministers of all dencminations in their work for that institution. The object of all was to unite for the general good. He was also pleased that the laity had taken such a promi- nent part in helping forward the movement for the extension of that most excellent institution. (Applause). The Rev. JOHN YONGE thanked the assembly for drinking the health of the Nonconformist ministers,for they certainly needed health for the due performance
