Davenport, Stockton Heath The CHAIRMAN responded. Their action had, he said, been endorsed by the town and neighbourhood and all the friends of Warrington. They had collected over £ll,OOO towards the £15,000 at which they were aiming and they felt sure the generosity, kindness, and charity of Warrington were by ilia means exhausted. (Applause). ,e 4 "THE IMPERIAL FORCES." is toast was proposed by the Rev. E. C, E. CA.RLETON who thought it was something in this materialising and money-getting age to feel that there were in our midst institutions like the army and navy I embodying sentiments and feelings which they shared; with another institution (the Church) whose existence i they all believed was some protest against the domina- tion of material things. Such common sentiments were patriotism,sacrifice, devotion and valour. Mr. Carleton referred with satisfaction to the response of Warring- , ton soldiers and volunteers to the demands made upon , them in the South African campaign and said our I imperial forces had beers v source of pride to English- men in the past, for their history exhibited a record which would compare with that of any other kingdom or Empire, ancient or modern. (Applause.) Colomel EDELSTEN responded. He said the army was supposed to exist chiefly for the purpose of causing wounds but he would remind that gathering that there was a large and increasing department in the army that was concerned with the healing of wounds. Never had man stricken in battle been better cared for than be was in the great conflict on the Manchurian slopes. If England had lagged behind, as she had such a tendency to do, he could state authoritatively that our present Secretary of State for War was doing his very utmost to remedy those deficiencies and to bring the medical department upto that of the Japanese. (Applause.) "LORD AND LADY LILFORD." Mr. W. PETER RYLANDS proposed the toast of "Lord and Lady Lilford " and gave some interesting facts as to the work of the Infirmary. During the year 1905 the number of cases treated exceeded 9,000. There were 537 inpatients, 304 operations, and 8,406 treated at the dispensary. That meant that more than 10 per cent. of the population of Warrington and of the surrounding district received help in time of need without any charge or practically without cost, at the hands of the institution. The work was done unostentatiously and with the best skill and medical resources at the disposal of the town. He was convinced that no one who had seen the work done or who had read the letters received from grateful patients could help feeling that the Infirmary was indeed a most deserving institution. It was well on that occasion that he should remind them of the magnificent gift by John Hatton of £lO,OOO, and of gifts totalling thousands of pounds given in the names of Beamont, Greenall, Parr, Walker, Crosfield and many others. But the generosity of Warrington was not exhausted yet, as was shown by the subscription list. If they all realized that the Infirmary had the first call upon them of all charitable institutions, remembering that charity began at home, he was certain the remain- ing sum would be cleared off easily before the opening day. (Applause). Lord and Lady Lilford had shown a very keen interest in the town and in the welfare of the Infirmary, and he wished them long life and prosperity and the best of health. (Applause). Lord LILFORD in returning thanks, said he was no stranger to Warrington. He had had the honour of taking part on more than one occasion in public ceremonies here and each time the townspeople had been good enough to receive him with a kindness and cordiality which, he could assure them, he would never forgot. The strikint, figures Mr. Rylands had quoted showed the real need for and usefulness of the institu- tion which he sincerely trusted would be an even greater boon in the future. (Applause.) "THE HONORARY MEDICAL OFFICERS." Captain CRoSFIELD proposed this toast and said the honorary staff included Dr. Fox, Dr. Joseph, Dr. Rich- mond, Dr. Bowden, Dr. Smith, Dr. E. J. Fox, and Dr. G. H. Joseph. These gentlemen, he said, gave a great amount of time gratis to attend to cases of poor people. During the last year they performed some 300 major eperations with only forty beds at their command,which showed that they had to work under very arduous circumstances. In these days when the gospel of" eat, drink and be merry" was preached so extensively and practised so energetically, it was stimulating and refreshing to come into touch with these instances of what they might call the higher Socialism. (Applause.) Dr. Fox in responding, said he occupied the proud position of being at the head of the medical depart- ment, after having served the institution for thirty years, twenty-five years as ordinary medical attendant and five years as consultant. The work of the staff had been considerably relieved by the ready co-operation of the Board of Management who had acceded to all reasonable demands placed before them. The real good work of the institution was done inside and therefore the extension would be of enormous benefit. He claimed that the medical profession stood as the highest donors to the institution. If they reckoned the 300 operations performed during the year at the modest figure of five guineas each it would mean about £1,500 saved in that way, alone. Multiply that by thirty and it would total close upon £45,000. How- ever it was a work of real love to the honorary staff, their desire being to benefit the people of Warrington. (Applause.)
"THE MAYOR." THE PERSONNEL OF THE COUNCIL.

Mr. JOHN FAIRCLOUGH proposed the health of "The Mayor," remarking that he had known his Worship for many years and considered him to be a very public- spirited man w. o was fully worthy of the office. (Applause). The MAYOR. in responding, expressed regret that more of the gentlemen of Warrington did not follow the example of their fathers and and serve the town by entering the Council. When he looked at the Council to-day he found it almost as it was when he came to WArrington thirty years ago, that many of the members were imruigint.ts and not the sons of those who occupied high positions in the town in bye- gone days. He hoped that more of the gentlemen he had indicated would come forward and help to make the name of Warrington as bright as that of any other town, for there was no reason why it should not be. They wanted men like his good friend Mr. Monks—(Applause)--and others who had done so much for Warrington. Unless they got in the Council Chamber better help than they had at the present time Warrington would still have thd ignominy of teing called one of the worst boroughs in Lancashire. The Mayor commended the efforts that were being put forth to beautify the town. They had opposition even to that movement but some of those who had some- thing higher than mere love of gain would persevere in their efforts to improve the surroundings of the poor people. (Applause). "TOWN AND TRADE OF WARRINGTON." MR. MONKS CRITICISES THE COUNCIL. Mr. J. D. BUCKTON briefly proposed this toast. Mr: F. MONKS responded, and said they all believed Warrington was one of the best towns in Lancashire. (Hear, hear.) As to its age, they would mat make any furtherinquiry than to say that they might put as many thousands to it as they liked. (Laughter.) For a long time Warrington was largely agricultural, but now it had become a centre of industry. As to the appeal the Mayor had made for the business men of the town to give their services, he for one failed to see that the town wanted them. He thought the recent agitation had practically driven all the best men into seclusion. What they were face to face with now was a class of Town Councillor who had not had the business experience and the practical knowledge which they all thought such a town as this required. He was surprised to-day to find that the latest candidate was a blacksmith in his own works. He did not know that he (the candidate) contributed very much to the rates, but he knew thut the firm did and that it was practically coming to this—that their own workmen were going to say how much rates they would have to pay. Whether that was a satisfactory state ot things or not'he would leave his hearers to judge. As far as trade was concerned, there were many men in that room who :were much interested in its ;prosperity. He believed it was very much better than at had been but ke did not think it was quite as good as they would like it. He was not going to touch on fiscal reform, because that subject was barred

break the connection between work and its reward you undermine the foundation of the spring of labour weaken the sources of activity, and enervate the will. Labour necessitates an effort against the instincts of idleness. Our wants are the incentive and the satis- faction of want the reward. If you dissociate the reward from the labour you remove the stimulus. There must be direct and proportionate connection between work and its reward ; in other words, the labourer must feel that the pr3duce of his labour is his own, and that he gets it. Activity would certainly decrease as there would be no immediate connection between the effort and its object. The producer must have the full enjoy- ment of his own creation. If the produce is entirely or even partially given to another, the intensity of labour will be lessened.

• I can best enforce this point by giving an illustra- tion from my own experience. I put a certain section of my works on piece work, I placed about 20 men in one gang, arranged to divide the product into so many parts, and to give to each man a certain number of parts, dividing these as fairly as I could according to the capacity of each man—that was paying each accord- ing to what I deemed to be his capacity to contribute to the sum total. The plan worked fairly well for a time, but soon I received complaints from the more active men, that some of those who were more indolent were not doing their share, and were practically reap- ing the advantage of the energy of the others. I then decided to divide the gang into two, giving to each gang a section of the work. Now on the Socialist theory the larger gang should have produced the larger result, because they were able to rk into each other's hands, each for the good of all. If one part were extra busy help could be given by a section in which the work might be slacker. I found contrary to the Socialistic theory that the two separate gangs did a good deal more work than the larger gang, and necessarily got more wages. The explanation is vary simple to those who know anything of human nature. If the man in the gang of twenty put in extra work he received the twentieth part of this extra in his reward. If a man in one of tha gangs of ten put in extra work he received twice as much or a tenth of the extra. To follow the experiment a little further, I found there was the same trouble in the gangs of ten. The sluggish still held back, and allowed the eager men to do the pushing. I again sub-divided this time into gangs of five. This was not so convenient for the work and if you take out the human element this further division ought, as in the first to have reduced the total output. Instead of this the output was appreciably increased. The reason being instead (V an individual receiving, as in the first case, the twentieth part of any extra work he put in, he now received a fifth. It was impossible to so divide the work as to pay each man for his individual work because some of the operations required two, and some four men to conduct, but if this difficulty had not stood in the way, and each man could have worked for and received his full reward there is little doubt that the total output would have been further increased. The active industrious man wouid have got all the extra reward for the extra work, while the sluggish man would know that he could not depend upon getting the result of the work of others, and could only get reward of the work of his own toil. Now the Socialist would have us make a gang not of five, ten, or twenty, but of all the workers of the State. Say the number is twenty million, the produce is to be divided equally or according to the need of each. Then the only material incentive that the individual would have to put in good lasting work would be that he would receive in reward a twenty millionth part. It is the general experience of those who have formed big associations that the most serious handicap to success is that the individual incentive is weakened by the size of the combination which gathers into one pool the result of the labours of so many. Once the connection is broken between labour and its reward not only will the slowest man set the pace but this pace will tend to de- crease indefinitely. Guarantee to the worker the full enjoyment of all he produces and you have a maximum of production. Give to each man his due,his produce, his whole produce, and nothing but his produce. This is the foundation of all justice ; it is what that enlightened conscience of all nations has made the basis of their moral law. It is a foundation upon which every social system should be built. Socialism does not propose to build upon this, but to revolutionize and abolish it. It introduces a new principle which destroys responsibility undermines justice, puts a premium on sloth, and paralyzes industry by cheating it out of its reward. The old imperatives are swept away, or become help- lessly enfeebled, and nothing enduring is put in their place.

div.head: SOCIALISM.
div.p: SOCIALISM.
MR. C. E. PARKER DISCUSSES THE QUESTION.

A well-attended meeting of the Junior Liberals was held on Monday evening under the chairmanship of Mr. Joseph Hawthorn. A paper on " Socialism" was given by Mr. Charles E. Parker (President of the Warrington Liberal Association). Mr. PARKER said : —A fortnight ago in this room an admirable paper was read by Mr. Osborne entitled " Why I became a Socialist." This paper, together with the subsequent interesting discussion, forms a fitting introduction to the paper I propose to read to-night. I set aside the many Socialistic schemes which have been put before the world at various times, and in various lauds, and desire to concentrate your attention on the form approved by Mr. Osborne and those who supported him. The phase of Socialism advocated was of an economic order, and it was restricted to the industrial sphere. In brief, it was this, first, that the State should secure by purchase all the means of production including land and capital, and that the present holders of wealth should enjoy the interest upon that wealth only for their life ; second, that everyone should give to the State in labour according to his capacity, and should receive from the State according to his need ; in other words that Society organised as a State, . is to own all wealth, direct all labour, and distribute the pro- ceeds as the representatives of the State deem to he the requirements of each individual. Against these principles of, " from each according to his capacity, and to each according to his need" I intend to advo- cate the principle of "to each according to his produce, his entire produce, and nothing but his produce " and contend that this embodies a conception far more just, and far more practical than the Socialist scheme named. I hold that this is the only principle adapted to our human nature and to an organised society.
MUNICIPALIZED INDUSTRIES

It was contended a fortnight ago that the success of nationalizing or municipalizing certain industries such as the postal system, telegraph, gas, water, and roads, was sufficient to ensure that if all other forms of industry were nationalized or municipalized similar success would attend this extension. But it is scarcely necessary to point out that the industries already taken over by the people, are not worked on the principles of Socialism advocated by Mr. Osborne and his friends, for every worker receives, not accord- ing to his need, but according to the value of his con- tribution in labour. The State or municipality assesses the value of that contribution by the value which is established by the competitive system. And it is a pertinent question to ask, supposing the con- nection were broken between the reward and the value of the labour, would these enterprises, instead of being a source of profit and convenience to the community, not become a source a considerable loss? I contend that the success of certain municipalized industries worked on one principal is no guarantee of success if worked on an entirely different one.

But apart from this the character of the industry is a most important point. It is quite reasonable to expect that an established industry that has become largely a matter of routine like the production of gas which everybody uses, should be successful because any fault in the management, character, pressure, etc., of the gas can immediately be detected and public attention directed to it. But the success of the pro- duction of gas which is used in Warrington is no guarantee that the production of iron and wire to be used on the railways and farms in the Argentine, would be equally successful. In short, there are some industries which naturally lend themselves to success- ful municipalization like those already taken over,but there are are others which require for their success direct individual initiative both in manufacture and in distribution,such are not adapted for State control. This is specially true in the commencement of an industry, and in any new department. I could instance a number of industries which have been worked by the State or by the municipality which have proved, from an economic standpoint, great failures. Some of these have come under my personal observation. It is quite possible that the principle Of municipalizing or nationalizing might with safety be further extended, but I hold that this should be done. gradually, and after careful consideration of the conditions affecting each industry. It is for example, quite possible that it would be to the interest of the country to nationalize our railways and canals. We have the experience of other countTirn to guide us in this, and the results should be carefully considered. Personally about thin I have an open nind, though lam bound to acknow- ledge that the arguments are not all in favour of State control. I clearly recognise that individualism may in certain directions be carried too far, just as I think industrial Socialism may be carried to a dangerous point. The best State is where the true balance is maintained by the operation of both principles. There is truth in both and wisdom must be exercised in the application and limitations of the two principles, as in most things the path of safety may lie between the two.
SYSTEM OF PAYMENT UNDER SOCIALISM.

But to return to the axiom "from each according to his capacity; to each according to his need" I would have you note that according to this principle the connection which has existed in all ages and amongst all peoples, between labour and its reward is severed by this new idea. There is henceforth to be no vital connection between work and wages. The two things are to have no relation to each other. It is a man's need, not his work, that is to regulate his share of the total production. Let us follow the application of this principle in a typical case. A. and B. work side by side under the new conditions. We will suppose that physically they are equally able as far as capacity goes, their contribution to the general stock should be squab and the ,principle is "from each according to his capacity.' Their physical needs are, we will suppose, also equal so each man will get an equal share. A. is a man of an eager, active temperament, his soul is awake, he is a great reader and under individualistic conditions he was accustomed to work hard that his higher nature might get into companionship with the world's thinkers through their books—he worked and saved that he might buy such. B. on the other hand is a phelgmatic man, as long as he gets enough to eat and drink and time to sleep he is con- tent. He is not necessarily a bad, or even a hopelessly idle man, but is one who works only that he may get enough to supply his animal wants. Under the new system the phlegmatic, sluggish man B. will naturally obey his natural disposition, all the more because the necessity for toil is removed ; he is sure of getting according to his need. A. who is working alongside of him observes his disposition to "Ca Canny " and follows his example. This confirms what Mr. Osborne seemed to ridicule, but did not answer, viz.' that under State Socialism "The slowest man will set the pace." Or suppose before slowing down A. complains to the boss of his department that B. (who, remember, has equal physical capacity with A) is not putting his fair share of work in. The boss goes to B. and a conversa- tion something like the following takes place : Boss. Look here, 8., you'll have to hustle. A. here is doing far more work, and the Committee have scheduled the capacity of you two as equal. B. I'm doing quite as much as there is any need to. A. is doing more than his share, and if he is fool enough to it I'm not, and besides any little difference that my work can make in the whole. stock for distribution is neither here nor there, so what are you nagging ? Boss replies that he must bring his case before the Committee, and he would be made to work. B. replies, "All right, sonny, go ahead. Your precious Committee cannot dismiss me ; it must give me enough to eat, and cannot make me work harder if I don't want to." Boss. Perhaps the Committee will reduce your share. B. No ! No ! Chuck that. "To each according to his need" and not his work, is your rule, and if you are going to desert the principles we will have some of you Committee Johnnies shifted. Boss. But don't you see you are not playing the game. You are getting as much as A.and only doing half the work. B. I don't want to be unfair to my mate with the intellect. If he cares to sweat that be may be learned, why don't you pay him for his extra work. That's nothing more than justice. It's not me that's making the m I "cif ty or wants to be unfair to anyone' it's your blooming Socialism that's making all the hot her. That, or something like it, will occur in every work- shop in the land under the proposed regime, and I ask' Socialists how they are going to get over such difficul- ties ?

I do not know if I am right in assuming that in speak- ing of giving to each according to his need, his physical requirements are alone considered. Our Socialist friends will be able to tell us whether the intellectual and spiritual needs of different men are to be calculated by the Commitee in giving to each his separate reward, in other words, are a man's needs to be defined in terms of his moral and mental nature as well as his physical ? If it be so it will immensely complicate a problem already far too complicated, for how is a Committee of Managemett to gauge the moral needs of the individuals it controls? We are to give to each according to his needs, I,ut the needs of an individual, of his body, mind and spirit, are things which no outsider can determine, they have no limits, and are constantly expanding or contracting. Society may make a rough guess as to how much a man should eat, but who can tell what different minds will aspire to, and how they will labour if the reward they get will enable them to satisfy their highest needs? As soon as you

div.head: Tfig FOUNDATIONS OF SOCIA.LISM CIIALLENGED.
div.p: Tfig FOUNDATIONS OF SOCIA.LISM CIIALLENGED.

My critics may be ready to acknowledge that in the present condition of the development of the race the application of Socialistic principles would be impracti- cal, but claim that they are goals to which we should aim in the hope of being able at some far off time to attain unto them. But I would point out that the difficulty arises not so much from the evil in human nature but from conditions which are essential.and permanent characteristics in our nature, characteristics which no amount of development will alter. For example there will always be varieties of character ; there will be those who are active, and those who are not —indeed,the more the race advances these differences will become more marked and operative. It was admitted last fortnight by one of the Socialist speakers ' that in the present state of human nattiro Socialism might he n ourae, rAtiter than a blessing. I assume what was in the speaker's mind was that thocho,thi be gradually developed along altruistic lines, so that the spirit of sympathy and brotherly love should ulti- mately displace the desire to work for individual reward which at present governs, and by this means human nature would become so changed as to be capable of deriving through Socialism all the anticipated bless- ings. If I have rightly interpreted the thought,we are agreed that Socialism cannot be successful until human nature be changed, and the desire for individual posses- sion of the fruit of individual effort,exorcised from our natures. But I challenge the assumption upon which the above rests that the individual effort resulting in individual possession is a bad thing. It is is no such thing ; it springs out of the God-given instinct of self preservation. If a man hes any primary inalienable right at all he has a right to himself, springing ont of this right he has a right to what he himself produces. Since no one can produce without a free access to nature equal access must be given to all. With equality of access assured, surely it is just that a man should have his produce, his whole produce, but nothing but his produce. Having entered into possession of his own, then let his altruistic feelings have full play, and if, seeing his brother in need he shutteth up his bowels of compassion against him, how dwelleth God in him, or even the love of men ? The owning of what anyone has produced is not the evil thing, it is the selfishness waich hoards when others stand in need. But I ask, is there anything inherent in Socialism that makes for the reformation of the individual, anything that will elimi- nate selfishness from our nature ? It is a system which works from without and does not touch the citadel of a man's being, his will and heart. Socialism, however, demands for its economic success a regenerated humanity, but it cannot bring this about. Let the present social system be worked by a regenerated humanity, and it would, in my opinion, produce far better results than would Socialism, and for this reason, amongst others, under the present system each can be taught to help to bear his brother's burden, whereas under Socialism the needs of each are ministered to by an official Committee. The State official is the medium through which the needs are satisfied. There is no free-will offering from individual brotherly hearts. If you want to take all the soul out of a thing, hand it to paid officialism. Governmental direction and distribu- tion is a poor mechanical and unnatural substitute for the free play of individual action. And now in conclusion let us turn to what I claim to be the only just and workable rule for human society. "To each his produce, his whole produce, and nothing but his produce." Some critic may be ready and eager to challenge me with this question : Do you consider that the present system conforms to your own rule? The question is a pertinent one, and will receive my emphatic answer that I do not. Although I would add that it conforms in its results more closely to it than that Socialism advocated by Mr. Osborne. As a general rule under the present-system a man gets what he works for, gets his produce. But I readily admit that he dons not get " his whole produce" and in place of a man getting " nothing but his produce," many men are so placed ' in a position of advantage by our existing system that 1 they are able to lay hold of a great deal they never pro-duce. To take an instance that will be'familiar to all, because it is one which of late has received a great deal of attention. A community by collective laboar gives to land surrounding our large towns an enhanced value which the owners as such do not contribute, but are in a position to force the community to pay for the increase the - community has created. To put it in a 1 general form private ownership of natural elements 1 carries with it the Power of such owners to levy a tax upon all workers, since the use of natural elements is a necessary condition to enable us to work and to live. 1 The Socialist creed makes no distinction between the gifts of nature and the stored up toil of man which we call (-vital. To my mind this is one of the fundamental errors, and one which leads to great confusion of thought. From Socialist speakers I have again and again heard about the "tyranny of the capitalist system," but when the same speakers proceed to give instances they tell us of some natural monopoly, the existence of a hich is in no way due to capital in its economic sense—that is stored up labour. In conclu- sion, I era justified in assuming we are all anxious to arrive at the truth, and while I think the system of Socialism outlined a fortnight ago to be unworkable, to be unjust;and in its effects to be immoral, I desire to keep an open mind, and will be pleased to give an unprejudiced and sympathetic consideration to anything which those who differ with me care to advance. Mr. OSBORNE, in opening a discussion on Mr. Parker's views, said that he was somewhat surprised that Mr. Parker should have based his lecture on a reply to a question which was elicited at the close of his (Ur. Osborne's) lecture a fortnight ago. The principle of "Every man' according to his need," he personally was prepared to stand by. He could not speak on behalf of any recognized Socialist society. It was unfair for Mr. Parker to instance two industries in Ireland—peat fuel and tinned fraits—eaeh of which had been failures from an economic point of view whilst they were managed by the State but so soon as private enterprize worked them they had been profitable. Why not take some industries in England and Scotland, which countries

were not labouring under such industrial disadvantages as Ireland? Mr. Osborne protested against the use of the word "immoral" lodged by Mr. Parker against Socialism. If Mr. Parker's idea, that every man should be paid according to his produce, was going to benefit society, and rid it of capitalistic conditions, he was prepared to go with him, but under present conditions that was impossible. Profit would have to be elimin- ated altogether to accomplish that object and that was, he contended, altogether beside the question under the present system of Government. If the principle of every man being paid according to his needs was impracticable surely the principle of every man receiving the whole of his produce and nothing but his produce was also. What about the men who to-day produced nothing yet drove about in their motor cars? Socialists contended that capital should be owned by the State,for they recognized that in many instances the more capital a man had the more he wanted. Capitalists did not think so much of the lives that were sacrificed in the building up of wealth so long as they were drawing their dividends. Mr. Parker believed that all the natural elements should be nationalized. Was it unfair to ask that if he believed land, railways, and canals should be nationalized, why should not industries be nationalized ? If the principle was admitted, then the only question was as to how the workers should be paid when all the undertakings were nationalized.
- The discussion was also taken part in by Messrs H. Gray, Griffiths, Derbyshire, Jones, Tilling, Kendrick, Randles and Ford, and a vote of thanks to Hr. Parker concluded the proceedings.

div.head: WHITECROSS WARD VACANCY. Election Next— Monday.
div.p: WHITECROSS WARD VACANCY. Election Next— Monday.

On Monday next the electors of Whitecross Ward will be called upon to elect a representative on the Town Council in place of the late Councillor Brough. Contrary to general expectation the Conservatives have forced a contest at the eleventh hour, their nominee being Mr. James Broadhurst, blacksmith, of Liverpool-road. The Liberals have an excellent candidate in Mr. Joseph Hawthorn, a well-known journalist, of 27, Lovely-lane, and his workers are leaving no stone unturned to secure his return. Mr. Hawthorn, as a life-long resident in the Ward,can claim a special knowledge of its needs and in his election address, which we publish in another column, he makes it clear that he would do everything in his power to safeguard the interests of his constituents, secure standard wages for Corporation workmen, and purity of administration in all matters affecting the ratepayers. Mr. Hawthorn has of late taken an active part in political life, and he is chairman of the Junior Liberal Association. A meeting in support of his candidature will be held this (Saturday) evening in the Thewlis-street schools when the speakers will include Mr. Joseph Howes, Councillors Evans,Barton, and Barton, and the candidate. The polling will take place in St. Barnabas' school on Monday between the hours of S a.m and 8 p.m.

div.head: • DEATH OF MR. W. R. NEIL.
div.p: • DEATH OF MR. W. R. NEIL.

A painful sensation was caused in Warrington on Thursday by the news of the sudden death of Mr. William Russell Neil, of " Waverley," Grappenhall. The deceased gentleman, who was in his 3Sth year, was widely known in Warrington and on every hand was held in the highest respect. He had suffered for sometime from an affection of the throat but his untimely end was altogether unexpected and was due to the bursting of a blood vessel. A second son of Mr. Alexander Neil, of Eccles, he eatly in life became associated with Messes. Fletcher, Russell and Co., and ten years ago was placed upon the directorate. With the employees of the firm he was exceedingly popular and by his death they have lost a considerate master and friend..

To the general public he was principally known by reason of his staunch support of Northern Union football, he, for three years, haring occupied the presidency of the Warringtou Club. He took a great interest in the progress of the game and it was always a source of considerable pleasure to him that the Club succeeded in winning the Northern Union Cup during his occupancy of the presidential chair.
The funeral will take place at Grappenhall at one o'clock on Monday.

div.head: LOCAL WEDDINGS.
div.p: LOCAL WEDDINGS.
Potter—Wright.

There was a pretty wedding at St. Paul's Church on Thursday, the contracting parties being Miss Margaret Wright,l step-daughter of the late Mr. Thomas Gray, Whitefield-road, Stockton Heath, and Captain and Quartermaster A. F. G. Potter, one of the most highly respected officers of the local Volunteer Battalion, of Lovely-lane. The Rev. W. Bracecamp officiated. There was a good con- gregation, ineluding many of Captain Potter's fellow-officers in the Volunteers. The bride was becomingly attired in a grey costume, and was attended by one .bridesmaid, Miss G. Jewkes, who wore a costume of electric blue. Major F. M Appleton discharged the duties of best man. Mr. E. Wilkes presided at the organ and played appropriate selections, the hymn "The voice that breathed o'er Eden " being sung. After the ceremony the wedding breakfast was served at the Patten Arms hotel, and a large number of guests attended. Later in the day Captain and Mrs. Potter left for London and the South where the honeymoon will be spent. The bride wore a travelling costume of beaver. Numerous presents were received, including an antique tea service from Colonel J. Reid Walker, silver cigar box from officers of lst.Volunteer,Battalion South Lancashire Regiment, and a case of silver spoons, &c., from the office staffs of Dallam and King-street Breweries. Jackson—Adams.

The marriage took place, quietly, at Brigstock Parish Church, Northamptonshire, on Thursday of Dr. Robert Jackson, M.8.C.M., Cowley Hill, St. Helens and Miss Gwendoline Doris Adams, second daughter of Dr. Adams, Bewsey-road, Warrington. The ceremony was performed by the Rev. J. T. Sandlands, M.A., uncle of the bride.

div.head: GRAVEDIGGING RECORD.
div.p: GRAVEDIGGING RECORD.

The parish clerk and sexton of Stanford Rivers,Essex, Mr. J. Woolmore, on Wednesday completed sixty years' service. He succeeded his father, and the two between them have dug the graves of all the parishioners who have died during the last 100 years. The inhabitants ,have given him a handsome sum of money.

div.head: CROSFIELD'S DRAMATIC SOCIETY.
div.p: CROSFIELD'S DRAMATIC SOCIETY.
Successful Performances.

Crosfield's Amateur Dramatic Society is the youngest local organization of its kind but so enthusiastic are the members, that considerable progress has been made. This week an interesting series of performances has been given in the Works Dining Hall and the large audiences have much appreciated the work of the amateurs. The society does not soar very high in the selection of plays, but it is due to all concerned to state that the comedies produced have afforded great amuse- ment, while the one dramatic scene was quite thrilling in its intensity. I The week's performances opened on Monday when the comedy "Still waters run deep," was produced. The play presented none but ordinary features and the plot centred round a villain, a foolish but innocent wife, an elderly lady whose youthful infatuation had placed her in the category of the villain's victims, and a hero who is regarded as a simpleton and a nonentity until he, in the last act,frustrates the intentions of the would be destroyer of domestic happiness, and earns the undy- ing gratitude of all—except the villain. Dealing with the hero first Mr. J. E. Newns was the success of the evening Regarded as a person who is only fit to be led by the nose he submits to innumerable indignities in his own home with an unruffled calm. Proving how- ever that "he is not such a fool as he looks " "John Mildmay "comes out strong in the closing scenes and , displaying a masterful handling of affairs enforces his authority and takes his rightful place as head of his own home. His turning of the tables upon his strong-minded aunt and wresting from her the domestic dictatorship was one of the most effective scenes in the play and in 'it ho displayed a commendable appreciation of the possibilities of the part. Captain Hawksley (Mr. G. B. Deane) was perhaps too much of a villain and the • display of a little less feeling would probably have , improved an otherwise excellent rendering. The part of Mr. Potter an inoffensive and weak willed old ! gentleman was ably interpreted by Mr. F. E. Gartland , who achieved a distinct success, in fact he could not have been better placed. Mr. S. F. Welsby as Dunbilk had little to do and that little he did well. He however i should strive to remember that a raw Irishman always speaks with a brogue and the correcting of his lapses of Imemory in this respect would add much to the part. , Miss E. Darbyshire, as the strong minded Mrs. I Sternbold had a difficult role and whilst her acting was of a high standard she was a little weak in parts, particularly when she discovered that she is in the ' villian's power. The same remark applies to Miss L. Pooley who fell somewhat short in the emotional scones though the flirtation scene with Captain Hawksley - , could hardly have been better presented. On the whole the performance was a distinct success and the work was considerably in advance of previous years. Preceding "Still waters run deep" was an amusing farce "The Doctor's Patient" which was excellently presented. In this Mr. S. F. Welsby was hardly an ideal doctor his principal fault being defective pro- nunciation. Mr. F. E. Gartland and Miss L. Cank, led by the doctor to believe each other to be mad,provided ! great amusement and both played well. Miss S. Darbyehire as the doctor's wife was also a success. Mr. 'J. E. Newns took the part of an Irish man-servant admirably and in this piece also was one of the leading spirits. The curtain-raiser on Tuesday and Thursday evenings was the farce "Kiss in the dark" waich shows how maarimouial bliss received a check through the icailan.a; na the hasband and his peculiar device to put his wife s affections to tne tesf. maw Is much desperate and threatening language but all is smoothed over in the end. Mr. G. B. Deane was the life and soul of the piece as the exceedingly irate husband and took the part very credit- ably. Mr. H. Flood was well placed as Frank Fathom, although he might with advantage have infused a little more spirit into his acting. Miss V. Hewitt was at home in the role of Pettibone, while Miss S. Darbyshire as Mary and Miss E. Darbyshireas the unknown female were also successful.

The dramatic scene "Love for Gold" followed and this gave Mr. G. B. Deane scope to display his talents in another direction. His delineation of The Miser was most powerful,especially in the concluding passages when the guilty mind conjures up visions of the trial and execution and the wretched man falls dead. Mr. Deane must be complimented upon an exceptionally praiseworthy pourtrayal. Mr. J. E. Newns contributed not a little to the success of this item, as the burglar. The programme concluded with the farce " Did you ever send your wife to Camberwell" which centred round a series of domestic complications which must have amused even the most seriously-inclined individual. The audience was kept in a continuous roar of laughter, all the performers entering into the spirit of the play and taking their parts admirably. Mr. T. Knowles undoubtedly carried off first honours as Chesterfield Honeybun his acting Leing easy and natural. Mr. F.E. Gartland as the innocent but misguided Crank, did much to keep up the merriment and he was particularly good when he had to work himself into a frenzy and challenge the unsuspecting Honeybun to a duel. Miss E. Wright rose to the occasion as Mrs. Houeybun and Miss S. Darbyshire was a capital Mrs. Crank. A dis- tinct success was scored by Miss L. Cank as the severe Mrs. Jewell.

Each evening a choice selection of music was given by the works orchestra under the conductorship of Mr. F. J. Lord. Mr. T. Knowles was an efficient stage. manager and Mr. J.Dutton an energetic hon. sec.

MUNICIPAL RLROIION, ItIiBRUARY 4TO, 1907. 0 VIVI ELECIORS OF WHITECRatS WARD LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, A vacancy has occurred in the representation of your Ward on the Town Council by the death of Mr. Councillor Brough. The Liberal Ward Committee has unanimously invited me to become a candidate for the position, and. after careful consideration, I have decided to place my services at your disposal. For upwards of thirty years I have lived in the Ward and can theref,re legitimately claim to know something ot its requirements. The sparsely populated district of my early days is now covered with working-class dwell- ings and this steady growth of the neighbourhcod requires the continual vigilance of the Ward's repre- sentatives to see that the paving, lighting and sanitary arratitements are not neglected. It is satisfactory to find that the Ward is the healthiest in the town, and it will be my endeavour to see that all the features of municipal government which contribute to this happy state of affairs are continued, and if possible improved. I am in favour of a Standard Rate of Wages to all Corporation Workmen, believing that the Corporation should set an example in this respect. The Fair Wage Clause should be strictly adhered to in the letting of Corporation Contract S. To secure purity of adminia.ratiOn in all matters affecting the Ratepayers will be my earnest eadeavour. I do not intend to make fulsome promises of great municipal improvements regardless of the ratepaNers' Interests, but shall aim at all-round efficiency with economy. Confidently relying on your support at the poll on Monday next. I am, 27, Lovely-lane, Warrington, Yours faithfully. January 29th, 1907. Jo3llPti HAWTHiORN.

Warrington Bakers' Social, An enjoyable gathering in connection with the War- rington Branch of the Amalgamated Union of Co-operative Bak6rs was held on Saturday evening at the Blue Bell Inn, Horsemarket-street. Mr. W. Rathbone presided over the proceedings which followed the partaking of a hot-pot supper and said he was pleased the members had decided to have a recreation club under the name of "The Warrington General Bakers' Recreation Club." Different kinds of sport would be provided for the members, who in. a short time would have a football match, the pro- ceeds to be devoted to the expenses of the club. Mr. J. Grealey proposed the health of the guest of the evening, Councillor Steel. The toast was drunk with musical honours. Councillor Steel, in reply, said he had had a great deal of experience in friendly society work, and he found that there was nothing like the social side and he was pleased they were going to have a recreation club. An enjoyable evening was spent, songs being given by Messrs. H. Hickin- bottom, D. Jones, Eccleston, J. Howard, and Barnes, and a duet by Messrs. Greenhalgh and Shaw. The accempanit-t was Mr. Gorse the blind pianist.
